The wind speed forecasts from the local NWP model are provided on a grid perhaps \({20}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) square, every eight hours over a 48-hour time horizon. These are then translated (downscaled) to the wind farm site at the height of the turbines. In flat terrain this may be done by spatial interpolation but in more complex terrain a meso-scale model is used. Using this site wind speed, the wind farm output is then modelled taking into account local topography and loss of energy in wind turbine wakes. Model Output Statistics (MOS) are then used to refine the model by comparing its outputs with measurements from the wind farms of power output and wind speeds.

docs.title: Appendix A10 Simple calculations for the connection of wind turbines
A10.1 The Per-unit system
docs.text:
The per unit system (Weedy and Cory, 1998) is simply a technique used by electrical power engineers to simplify calculation by expressing all values as a ratio of:

  • actual value (in any unit);

  • base or reference value (in the same unit).

Its advantages include: (1) a reduction in the appearance of \(\sqrt{}3\) in the calculations (2) that similar per unit values apply to systems of various sizes and (3) by appropriate choice of voltage bases the solution of networks containing several transformers is facilitated.

For simple calculations, such as those required for assessment of a wind turbine or small wind farm on a simple distribution circuit, all that is required is to:

  1. Assume an arbitrary base VA (e.g. 10 MVA for a small wind farm connection).

  2. Select voltage bases of each voltage level of the network (e.g. \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) and \({11}\mathrm{{kV}}\) ). These voltage bases should be related by the nominal turns ratios of the transformers.

  3. Calculate the appropriate real and reactive power flows at the generator terminals in per unit (i.e. for a Power flow of \(5\mathrm{{MW}}\) with the base VA chosen as \({10}\mathrm{{MVA}}\) , the per unit value is \(P = 5/{10}\) or 0.5 per unit. Similarly for a Reactive Power flow of \(1\mathrm{{MVA}}r\) the per unit value is \(Q = 1/{10}\) or 0.1 per unit).

  4. If necessary transform the impedances of the circuit from ohmic to per unit values using a base impedance of \({Z}_{\text{ base }} = {V}^{2}{}_{\text{ base }}/V{A}_{\text{ base }}\) .

  5. The base current at any particular voltage level is calculated from: \({I}_{\text{ base }} = V{A}_{\text{ base }}/ \; \sqrt{}3 \times {V}_{\text{ base }}\) .

docs.title: A10.2 Power flows, slow voltage variations and network losses
docs.text:
If the output from a distributed wind turbine generator is absorbed locally by an adjacent load then the effect on the distribution network voltage and losses is likely to be beneficial. However, if it is necessary to transport the power through the distribution network then increased losses may occur and slow voltage variations may become excessive (Jenkins, Ekanayake and Strbac, 2010).

If the wind generator operates at unity power factor (i.e. Reactive Power \(Q = 0\) ), then the voltage rise in a lightly loaded radial circuit (Figure A10.1) is given approximately by:

\[ {\Delta V} = {V}_{1} - {V}_{0} = {PR}/{V}_{0} \tag{A10.1} \]

Operating the generator at a leading power factor (absorbing reactive power) acts to reduce the voltage rise but at the expense of increased network losses. In this case the voltage rise is given by:

\[ {\Delta V} = {V}_{1} - {V}_{0} = \left( {{PR} - {XQ}}\right) /{V}_{0} \tag{A10.2} \]

Figure A10.1 Fixed-speed wind turbine on a radial circuit

The impedance of an overhead \({11}\mathrm{{kV}}\) distribution circuit may, typically, have a ratio of inductive reactance to resistance \((X/R\) ratio) of 2 . An uncompensated induction generator at rated output, typically, has a power factor of 0.89 leading, that is, \(P = - {2Q}\) . Thus, under these conditions, there is no apparent voltage rise in the circuit at full power. However, the real power loss \(\left( W\right)\) in the circuit is given approximately by:

\[ W = \left( {{P}^{2} + {Q}^{2}}\right) R/{V}_{0}^{2} \tag{A10.3} \]

The reactive power drawn by the generator acts to limit the voltage rise but higher real power losses are incurred in the connecting circuit.

Equations A10.1-A10.3 for voltage rise and circuit losses are approximate only and do not apply to heavily loaded circuits. A simple but precise calculation for voltage rise in any radial circuit may be carried out using an iterative technique.

Complex quantities are indicated by bold type.

At the generator busbar of Figure 10.9 the apparent power (sometimes known as the complex power) \({S}_{1}\) is given by:

\[ {\mathbf{S}}_{1} = P - {jQ} \tag{A10.4} \]

(for a generator operating at lagging power factor, exporting VArs, \({\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{1}}\) would be given by \(P + {jQ})\)

By definition \(\mathbf{S} = {\mathbf{{VI}}}^{ * }\) . * indicates the complex conjugate (i.e. the sign of the imaginary component of the complex number is reversed).

Therefore, the current flowing in the circuit is given by:

\[ \mathbf{I} = {\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{ * }/{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{ * } = \left( {P + {jQ}}\right) /{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{ * } \tag{A10.5} \]

The voltage rise in the circuit is given by \(\mathbf{{IZ}}\) and so:

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}} = {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}} + \mathbf{{IZ}} = {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}} + \left( {R + {jX}}\right) \left( {P + {jQ}}\right) /{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{ * } \tag{A10.6} \]

It is common for the network voltage \({\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}}\) to be defined and the generator busbar voltage \({\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}\) required. \({\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}\) can be obtained using the simple iterative expression:

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{\left( n + 1\right) } = {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}} + \left( {R + {jX}}\right) \left( {P + {jQ}}\right) /{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{*\left( n\right) } \tag{10.7} \]

where \(n\) is the iteration number.

This is a simple form of the conventional Gauss-Seidel load flow algorithm (Weedy and Cory, 1998). Once the calculation converges an accurate solution is obtained. More complex load flow calculations may be carried out using commercially available power system analysis programs. These include models of transformers, with their tap changers, and can solve large interconnected circuits in only a few iterations using more advanced algorithms.

Example: Calculation of voltage rise in a radial circuit

Figure A10.2 Example of calculation of voltage rise on a radial circuit (all values in per unit)

Consider a 5 MW wind farm operating at a power factor of 0.98 leading. The network voltage \(\left( {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{0}}\right)\) is \(\left( {1 + {j0}}\right)\) per unit and the circuit impedance \(\left( \mathbf{Z}\right)\) is \(\left( {{0.05} + {j0.1}}\right)\) per unit on a 10 MVA base (Figure A10.2).

A power factor of 0.98 leading implies a reactive power draw of 1.01 MVAr.

Thus, following Equation A10.7 the calculation becomes

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{\left( n + 1\right) } = 1 + \left( {{0.05} + {j0.1}}\right) \left( {{0.5} + {j0.101}}\right) /{\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{*\left( n\right) } \]

For the first iteration \(\left( {n = 0}\right)\)

Assume

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{*\left( 0\right) } = 1 + {j0} \]

then \({\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{\left( 1\right) }\) may be calculated to be:

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{\mathbf{1}}^{\left( 1\right) } = {1.0149} + {j0.0551} \]

For the second iteration \(\left( {n = 1}\right)\)

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{*\left( 1\right) } = {1.0149} - {j0.0551}\text{ then } \] \[ {\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{\left( 2\right) } = {1.0117} + {j0.0549} \]

For the third iteration \(\left( {n = 2}\right)\)

\[ {\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{*\left( 2\right) } = {1.0117} - {j0.0.0549}\text{ then } \] \[ {\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{\left( 3\right) } = {1.0117} + {j0.0551} \]

and the procedure has converged.

Therefore \({\mathbf{V}}_{1} = {1.013}\) per unit at an angle of \({3}^{ \circ }\) , that is, the voltage at the generator terminals is \({1.3}\%\) above that at the source. The angle between the two voltage vectors is small \(\left( {3}^{ \circ }\right)\) .

The approximate calculation \(\left( {{V}_{1} = {V}_{0} + \text{ PR-XQ }}\right)\) indicates a voltage \({V}_{1}\) of 1.015 per unit (i.e. a rise of 1.5%). This is confirmed by the results of the first iteration.

The current (I) in the circuit may be calculated from:

\[ \mathbf{I} = {\mathbf{S}}_{1}^{ * }/{\mathbf{V}}_{1}^{ * } = \left( {{0.5} + {j0.101}}\right) /\left( {{1.0117} - {j0.0551}}\right) \] \[ = {0.4873} + {j0.1264}\text{ per unit } \] \[ \left| \mathbf{I}\right| = {0.503}\text{ per unit } \]

With a connection voltage of \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) the base current is given by

\[ {I}_{\text{ base }} = V{A}_{\text{ base }}/\sqrt{}3 \times {V}_{\text{ base }} = 5 \times {10}^{6}/{1.732} \times {33} \times {10}^{3} = {87.5}\text{ Amps } \]

and so the magnitude of the current flowing in the \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) circuit is \({44}\mathrm{{Amps}}\) .

The real power loss in the circuit \(\left( W\right) {\text{ is }}^{3}\) :

\[ W = {I}^{2}R = {0.0127}\text{ per unit or }{127}\mathrm{\;{kW}} \]

The symmetrical short-circuit level at the generator busbar, before connection of the generators is simply:

\[ {S}^{\prime \prime } = 1/\left| \mathbf{Z}\right| = 1/{\left( {0.05}^{2} + {0.1}^{2}\right) }^{1/2} \] \[ {S}^{\prime \prime } = {8.94}\mathrm{{pu}}\text{ or }{89.4}\mathrm{{MVA}} \]

Once the induction generators of a wind farm are connected then they will make a contribution to the short-circuit current seen by a circuit breaker when it closes on to a fault. This is typically some five times the rating of a directly connected fixed speed induction generator, for example some 25 MVA in this case, giving a total short-circuit level of 115 MVA. However, for a three-phase symmetrical fault the fault current contribution from an induction machine decays rapidly and will make only a small contribution to the fault current which must be interrupted by an opening circuit breaker. Detailed guidance on the calculation of fault currents, including the contribution from induction generators is given in IEC 60909.

\({}^{3}\) Note when the calculations are carried out using the per-unit system this is the aggregated power loss of all three phases.

docs.title: 11 Offshore wind turbines and wind farms
11.1 Development of offshore wind energy
docs.text:
Offshore wind energy is developing rapidly (Figure 11.1) with a total installed capacity in 2010 of approximately 3000 MW, some 1.5% of worldwide wind farm capacity. In a number of Northern European countries it is increasingly difficult to obtain permission to construct large wind farms onshore and this has stimulated interest in moving offshore, into the North Sea and Baltic. To meet its greenhouse gas emission targets, the UK has ambitious plans for some 15-20,000 MW of offshore wind farm capacity by 2020 with some projects more than \({100}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) offshore in average water depths of \({50}\mathrm{\;m}\) . The advantages of locating wind farms offshore include:

  • Large areas are available for wind farm development with limited environmental impact.

  • Mean wind speeds are high and this gives high capacity factors.

  • Wind turbulence is low.

  • Landfalls of the cables and points of connection to the power network are close to cities and load centres.

Figure 11.1 shows the development of world-wide capacity of offshore wind farms. Until around 2000 the projects were small and located in rather shallow water less than \(5\mathrm{\;{km}}\) from shore. Then larger wind farms began to be constructed, in particular the two large Danish wind farms at Horns Rev (160 MW, 2002) and Nysted (166 MW, 2003). Presently a number of wind farms of up to 500 MW are being constructed in Northern Europe, particularly off the UK with smaller installations in the Far East, particularly off the coast of China (Table A11.1).

Wind Energy Handbook, Second Edition. Tony Burton, Nick Jenkins, David Sharpe and Ervin Bossanyi.

© 2011 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. Published 2011 by John Wiley & Sons, Ltd. ISBN: 978-0-470-69975-1

Figure 11.1 Offshore wind farm capacity worldwide (1991-2012)

Offshore installations represent a small fraction of the total wind power market and so the turbines are generally marinised developments of the machines used onshore (rated at up to 3.6 MW) but with some larger turbines (up to 5 MW) used in deep water sites. There is also one installation of two floating wind turbines. In depths of water of up to \({20}\mathrm{\;m}\) , either monopile or gravity foundations have been used while jacket or tripod structures are used for deeper waters. For smaller wind farms close to shore, the wind farm power collection cables at \({30} - {36}\mathrm{{kV}}\) are extended to shore. Larger wind farms use an offshore transformer station while High Voltage Direct Current transmission will be used for very large remote projects. Access for maintenance is generally by boat although helicopters have been used in some projects.

Table 11.1 shows an indicative breakdown of the capital costs of an offshore wind farm project. The turbines make up a rather lower fraction of the costs than for an onshore project with the support structures, cables and electrical connection a greater proportion. Installation of equipment offshore is, of course, a significant cost.

Table 11.1 Typical breakdown of costs for an offshore wind farm (after EWEA, 2009)

Element of offshore wind farm% of total costWind turbines51Support structures19Cables and network connection (including installation)15Installation of turbines and support structures9Other capital costs6

The disadvantage of installing wind turbines offshore is the higher capital and operating costs and these have shown a considerable increase over the short history of offshore wind power development. This increase in costs has been studied by Gross et al., 2010. From 2002 to 2004, capital costs for UK offshore wind farms were relatively stable at less than \(\textsterling {1.5}\mathrm{\;m}/\mathrm{{MW}}\) . However, since then capital costs have doubled to \(\textsterling 3\mathrm{\;m}/\mathrm{{MW}}\) with the lev-elised costs of electrical energy increasing from £85/MWh (2004) to £150/MWh (2010). This compares with a capital cost for onshore wind energy of between \(\textsterling {1.3}\mathrm{\;m}/\mathrm{{MW}} - \textsterling {1.8}\) m/MW and a levelised cost of energy of £94/MWh (DECC, 2010). The comparable lev-elised cost of electrical energy in the UK from Combined Cycle Gas Turbine generators was £80/MWh (2010).

Thus, although onshore wind energy can be considered the most cost-effective low carbon technology for electricity generation, offshore wind energy is expensive requiring considerable additional support. \({}^{1}\)

Gross et al., 2010 considered that the factors that drove the escalation in cost of UK offshore wind farms from the mid-2000s to 2009 have been (in descending order of impact):

  1. Materials, commodities and labour costs.

  2. Currency movements.

  3. Increasing prices for turbines over and above the cost of materials, due to supply chain constraints, market conditions and engineering issues.

  4. The increasing depth and distance of more ambitious projects, affecting installation, foundation and operation and maintenance (O & M) costs.

  5. Supply chain constraints, notably in vessels and ports.

  6. Planning and consenting delays.

There has recently been some evidence of a small drop in capital costs of UK wind farms from £3 m/MW (2009) to £2.9 m/MW (2010) with a best guess of a cost of energy of £115/MWh by the mid-2020s. Some projects in the Baltic in rather shallow, sheltered waters close to shore have reported lower costs. Consideration of costs and other commercial matters is difficult and any analysis dates very quickly. However, it would appear that the early experience of UK offshore wind farms in rather shallow waters often close to shore gave a rather optimistic view of costs and that the later larger wind farms in more demanding exposed, offshore environments will lead to a higher cost of electrical energy unless considerable innovation is employed to reduce both capital and operating costs.

Offshore wind energy is in its infancy and experience is being gained as wind farms are constructed further from the shore and in more demanding environments. A number of books and reports on offshore wind energy are now emerging. Offshore climatology and meteorology are discussed by Barthelmie et al. and access by Dalen and Jakobsson in the comprehensive book on offshore wind power by Twidell and Gaudiosi (2009). Ackerman (2005) addresses offshore electrical systems while Hau (2006) provides an overview of the subject. After a review of offshore wind meteorology, this chapter considers the design loads of offshore wind turbines, which differ significantly from those onshore. The design of support structures is described including fatigue calculations for monopile foundations while particular aspects of offshore power collection systems are also addressed.

\({}^{1}\) Electricity generated from UK offshore wind farms attracts two Renewable Obligation Certificates or double the support of electricity generated from onshore wind farms.

docs.title: 11.2.1 The structure of winds offshore
docs.text: For sites far from shore, and for near-shore sites when the wind is blowing from open sea to land, mean wind speeds are usually higher than on land due to the absence of obstructions to the flow. Similarly, turbulence levels are usually much lower than on land, with low wind shear corresponding to the small surface roughness. However, the surface roughness increases with wave height, so turbulence and wind shear may be much higher during periods of large waves. These are correlated with periods of strong winds, since the waves are generally wind-driven, but there may be a significant time lag, so a wind farm may experience low winds in conjunction with high waves following a storm out at sea. Also the lower frequency swell waves may travel long distances, and may have been caused by high winds elsewhere which may never reach the wind farm. The contribution of the wind to the design loads of offshore turbines is considered in Section 11.3.2.

docs.title: 11.2.2 Site wind speed assessment
docs.text:
Quantification of the long-term wind resource at a potential wind farm site plays a central role in determining the economic feasibility of a project. For onshore wind farms this is typically achieved through the collection of wind data from an onsite meteorological mast and/or analysis of energy production data from neighbouring operational projects (Section 9.1.3, Chapter 9) These datasets are typically analysed in conjunction with historical records from a local meteorological station, regional wind index or modelled hindcast source as well as site wind flow models in order to predict the long-term wind climate at the site.

A similar approach may be adopted for offshore wind projects although there are significantly higher costs associated with the erection of meteorological masts at sea. Alternatively, wind resource estimates may be based on secondary sources such as measured wind data obtained from neighbouring sites or publicly funded measurement stations in the region of interest. In such circumstances, the wind analyst must assess the difference in wind climate between the reference mast and the target site, as well as the uncertainty associated with this assessment.

A commonly held assumption has been that the horizontal spatial variation of long-term mean wind speed in the offshore environment is relatively limited (Barthelmie 1993; Coelingh et al., 1996). Therefore, the uncertainty associated with extrapolation of measurements from one physical location to another has often been perceived as relatively limited. However, in the absence of high quality public domain data from several reliable measurement nodes, there is little evidence for this assumption and so wind climate prediction is subject to a significant degree of uncertainty in the absence of a high quality measurement campaign on the site of interest. This can have a significant impact on the outlook for the financing of some projects.

Various methodologies may be applied in order to assess the variation of wind resource across wide areas of the offshore environment. These include conventional computational flow modelling techniques such as WAsP (Mortensen et al., 1993) as well as more sophisticated modelling including Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Mesoscale methods. The latter is an increasingly applied technique which is based on Numerical Weather Prediction models developed by the meteorological research community. A Global Climate Model is used to find the conditions of the upper atmosphere and these results are then either used as boundary conditions of Regional Climate Models (at a scale typically of \({50}\mathrm{\;{km}} \times {50}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) ) or with empirically derived relationships with the sea surface parameters, temperature and wind speed (Barthemie et al. in Twidell and Gaudiosi, 2009). The benefit of this approach is the potential for capturing the wide scale synoptic trends as well as more localised thermal and topographic effects through application of a theoretically robust meteorological model, initiated from a large database of historical observations.

Analysis of images recorded by satellite-mounted instrumentation is also becoming a more frequently applied methodology for considering the variation in offshore wind resource. One of the most commonly utilised instruments is a Scatterometer, which is an active microwave device used to derive estimates of wind speed and direction based on returns from a fan beam of short pulses. These returns are received at a variety of incidence angles which respond principally to the surface roughness of the sea. When the wavelength of the incident beam is in phase with the wavelength of the short-crested localised 'wind waves' (taking account of the incident beam angle), resonant signals become present in the backscatter return (Aage et al., 1998). The intensity of the resonant backscatter is proportional to the steepness of the wind waves and hence also to the localised wind speed at the time of observation. The relationship between the magnitude of resonant backscatter and wind speed has been derived empirically and also takes into consideration the incidence angle and the azimuth angle of the satellite observation direction with respect to the wind direction (Aage et al., 1998). Whilst the absolute accuracy of the derived wind speed values is limited by the validity of the empirically-derived relationship applied and the availability of the data is limited due to infrequent spatial and temporal sampling, analytical methods have been developed that allow a robust estimate of the spatial variation of wind resource over domains of several hundred kilometres to be determined (Phillips et al., 2008).

In summary, a wide variety of measurement and computer model-based applications are available to determine the wind resource at any given offshore wind site. The uncertainties associated with the source data and analytical methodology adopted play a significant role in determining the level of confidence that may be ascribed to projections of long-term energy production, which in turn has a substantial influence on the economic viability of any given offshore wind farm development.

docs.title: 11.2.3 Wakes and array losses in offshore wind farms
docs.text:
Wake losses in offshore wind farms can lead to a considerable loss of energy particularly at wind speeds below rated. Wake losses are most strongly dependent on wind speed through the turbine thrust coefficient, being high at low wind speeds and then decreasing as wind speeds increase. Above rated wind speed, pitch regulated turbines limit their power production by feathering the blades, which reduces the thrust coefficient and hence the wake losses at downstream turbines, so above a certain wind speed all turbines may be producing rated power despite the wakes. Stall regulated turbines continue to have a high thrust coefficient, which may cause high wake losses at all wind speeds.

The thrust coefficient implies an extraction of momentum from the air flow, but further downstream the momentum is replenished by mixing from the higher-speed flow above the wind farm. Atmospheric boundary layer models can provide ways of calculating the rate of momentum replenishment, from which the efficiency of the wind farm can be calculated (Bossanyi, 1980). However, a more detailed assessment should consider the development of the individual turbine wakes and their interaction with downstream turbines. This means that the wake losses depend significantly on wind direction as well as turbine spacing. With a regular array of turbines, the wake losses will be high in certain narrow wind direction sectors, and the overall average losses will depend on the joint distribution of wind speed and direction.

Array wake losses can be exacerbated by small separation distances of the turbines used in some projects and may be related to the low levels of ambient turbulence of the offshore wind (Barthelmie et al., 2005). For example, the Lillgrund offshore wind farm (Figure 11.2) was built with 48,2.3 MW, \({93.5}\mathrm{\;m}\) diameter turbines (Dahlberg and Thor,2009). It was constructed with rather small separation distances between turbines (3.3 D along each row and 4.4 D between rows). The small separation distances arose as the rotor diameter of the available offshore turbine was increased by the manufacturer during the wind farm permitting process when the base positions had been fixed. An extensive campaign of measurements showed that for wind blowing directly down a row, the second turbine experienced a power deficit wake loss of \({80}\%\) (i.e. it produced only \({20}\%\) of the power of the first turbine over a range of wind speeds below rated). Similarly at a spacing of 4.4 D the power deficit was around 70%.

Figure 11.2 Lillgrund wind farm layout. Dahlberg and Thor, 2009. Reproduced by permission of Vattenfall

Figure 11.3 Lillgrund wind farm: variation in array efficiency with wind direction for wind speeds below rated. Dahlberg and Thor, 2009. Reproduced by permission of Vattenfall

Figure 11.3 shows how the wind farm array efficiency varies with wind direction for wind speeds below rated. The array efficiency (relative power) is defined as the average array power generation per turbine at a given wind speed divided by the corresponding output of a turbine not suffering from wake losses - that is, one at the windward edge of the array. Pronounced dips when the wind is blowing along the rows are clearly seen. On the assumption of an istropic wind direction probability distribution, the overall array efficiency of the wind farm was estimated to be \({67}\%\) for wind speeds below rated and \({77}\%\) for a site wind speed distribution assumed to be Rayleigh with an annual mean of \(8\mathrm{\;m}/\mathrm{s}\) . This implies that the power output of this rather dense offshore wind farm was reduced by approximately 23% compared to what might be expected from a single isolated turbine (Lillgrund Pilot Project, 2008). Wake losses at Middelgrunden (curved single line of turbines, spacing 2.4 D) were reported as around 10% in (Barthelmie et al., 2007).

The Lillgrund wind farm was exceptional in its small spacing between turbines. Horns Rev has spacing of 7 D along its rows and 10 D between rows. Its output has been analysed (Hansen K et al., 2010) to show maximum power deficit wake loss of the second wind turbine in the array of around \({40}\%\) at wind speeds of 5-9 m/s dropping to \({30}\%\) at 11-13 \(\mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}\) for a narrow range of directions. The flow deficit sector generated by each turbine was approximately 25-30°. Overall array losses were reported as 12.4% (Sørensen et al., 2006).

Atmospheric turbulence and stability can have a significant effect on wake losses (Barthelmie and Jensen, 2010). Turbulent mixing causes the velocity deficit in the wake to broaden and weaken as it convects downwind, and with the low levels of turbulence typical of some offshore sites the individual wakes will persist further downstream, but their effects will be felt over a narrower range of wind directions.

A number of approaches have been used to predict offshore array efficiency. Barthelmie et al. (2009) compare six different models. The simplest model uses a simple 'top-hat' wake profile, which is assumed to expand linearly based on a wake decay coefficient. Somewhat more sophisticated is the use of wake models derived from the Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations together with empirical relationships for the wake-generated turbulence and the superposition of multiple wakes; while two of the models use full Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) modelling of the flow through the wind farm, treating the rotor disks as momentum sinks. The Barthelmie et al. paper notes that although most of the accepted wake models appear to give reasonable results for single wakes or small wind farms, wake losses are under-predicted in large offshore arrays. This is thought to be due to inadequate representation of turbulence induced from the upstream turbines and the effect of atmospheric stability. On land such effects tend to be masked by the higher levels of turbulence caused by the topography. The performance of all models can be improved by modified parameterizations (Barthelmie et al., 2010; Cleve et al., 2009; Schlez and Neubert, 2009) although research is continuing to better understand and predict the flow and wakes in offshore wind farms.

On a larger scale, as more offshore wind farms are built the effect of the 'wake' of an entire wind farm on the energy production of another wind farm starts to be of interest, as well as the effect this may have on the total wind energy resource which can be extracted from a given sea area. This is proving difficult to assess, partly due to the lack of measurements. Results summarized in (Frandsen et al., 2009) suggest that a variety of modelling approaches may be appropriate but still need further verification if they are to be used successfully to estimate power output prior to wind farm construction.

docs.title: 11.3.1 International Standards
docs.text:
National design standards specifying wind and wave loadings on offshore structures were developed as North Sea oil began to be exploited, and were subsequently utilised for the design of the first offshore wind farms. However, offshore wind turbines differ from offshore oil platforms in that the wind loading on wind turbine support structures is a much more significant element of the total loading than is the case for oil platforms, so the desirability of design standards tailored to offshore wind turbines was soon recognised.

The first design standard for offshore wind turbine structures to appear was published by Det Norske Veritas in 2004. Offshore Standard DNV-OS-J101, 'Design of Offshore Wind Turbine Structures', is a comprehensive document, covering marine conditions, design load cases, wave loading and structural design. The design load cases were the same as those set out in IEC 61400-1, but with appropriate wave heights or sea states specified. However, in 2007, a revised edition was published with the load cases modified to be consistent with those in the draft IEC 61400-3 (see below).

Germanischer Lloyd published Guidelines for the Certification of Offshore Wind Turbines in 2005. It covers the rotor and nacelle components as well as the support structure and is structured in the same way as the parallel document for onshore machines, but with individual chapters expanded to include the requirements particular to offshore siting.

The International Electrotechnical Commission standard IEC 61400-3 'Wind Turbines - Part 3: Design requirements for offshore wind turbines' appeared in 2009. Unlike the GL guidelines referred to above, this is not a stand-alone document, but has to be read in conjunction with IEC 61400-1 (see Chapter 5).

The load cases specified in IEC 61400-3 closely correspond to those in IEC 61400-1, with the marine conditions to be taken into account added in each case. Deterministic waves may be considered in conjunction with deterministic gusts in a few load cases, but in most the standard specifies stochastic sea states and turbulent wind, requiring several ten-minute simulations to be run. A minimum of six such simulations is required for each mean hub height wind speed and sea state for each load case, but for some load cases significantly greater numbers are required. The wind and marine conditions specified are considered in the next sections.

Some of the work in developing the IEC 61400-3 guidelines was carried out under the auspices of a European Community supported R & D project 'Recommendation for Design of Offshore Wind Turbines' (contract no ENK5-CT-2000-00322), or RECOFF, and was reported in some 70 papers.

docs.title: 11.3.2 Wind conditions
docs.text:
IEC 61400-3 requires the support structure to be designed for site-specific wind conditions, but, in the case of the rotor-nacelle assembly, the alternative approach of designing for one of the wind turbine classes defined in IEC 61400-1 may also be followed.

The following hub height wind parameters are to be determined at the site, preferably by site monitoring:

  • the extreme ten-minute mean wind speed with a recurrence period of 50 years, \({U}_{ref}\) ;

  • wind speed and direction distributions;

  • turbulence intensity for wind speeds over the operating range, and at \({U}_{ref}\) ;

  • standard deviation of turbulence intensity at each wind speed;

  • wind shear;

  • air density.

In the absence of site monitoring, the above parameters may be estimated from local standards, or, in the case of turbulence intensity, from the surface roughness parameter, \({z}_{o}\) . Sea roughness increases with wind speed, and \({z}_{o}\) may be estimated from the Charnock expression:

\[ {z}_{o}\left( \bar{U}\right) = \frac{{A}_{c}}{g}{\left\lbrack \frac{\kappa \bar{U}}{\ln \left( {{z}_{\text{ hub }}/{z}_{o}\left( \bar{U}\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack }^{2} \tag{11.1} \]

where \({A}_{c}\) is Charnock’s constant, \(g\) is the acceleration due to gravity and \(\kappa\) is von Karman’s constant (0.4). The standard recommends values of \({A}_{c}\) ranging between 0.011 for open sea and 0.034 for near-coastal locations. The design value of turbulence intensity is taken as the 90% quantile given by the equation:

\[ {I}_{u} = 1/\ln \left( {{z}_{\text{ hub }}/{z}_{o}\left( \bar{U}\right) }\right) + {1.28}\left( {{1.44}{I}_{15}}\right) /\bar{U} \tag{11.2} \]

Figure 11.4 Variation of turbulence intensity with wind speed - onshore and offshore

The first term in this expression is an accepted formula for the mean turbulence intensity and the second term represents the additional 1.28 standard deviations of turbulence intensity required for the \({90}\%\) quantile. Accordingly \({I}_{15}\) can be estimated as \(1/\ln \left( {{z}_{hub}/{z}_{o}\left( {15}\right) }\right)\) .

The resulting variations in turbulence intensity with wind speed at open sea and near-coastal locations are compared with that at an onshore site with medium turbulence (Category B) in Figure 11.4. It is seen that the turbulence intensity at an offshore coastal location is only slightly higher than over the open sea, but in both cases is significantly less than that onshore throughout the operational speed range of typically \(5 - {25}\mathrm{\;m}/\mathrm{s}\) .

docs.title: 11.3.3 Marine conditions
docs.text:
The marine conditions relevant to support structure design encompass waves, currents, water level and, where appropriate, scour, seabed movement and sea ice. In the case of the IEC 61400-3 operational load cases which have their counterparts in IEC 61400-1 (i.e. all but load case 1.6), normal marine conditions are specified, with severe marine conditions applicable in load case 1.6 and extreme conditions applicable in a number of non-operational load cases.

The wave climate is most accurately described in terms of a stochastic sea state model but, in view of the non-linearity of wave loading models in storm conditions, it is necessary to introduce deterministic design waves as well. The various sea states defined in IEC 61400-3, and the alternative deterministic design waves, are described in succeeding sections, together with details of the co-existent currents and water levels to be considered. Before moving to these, however, the wave spectra commonly employed in stochastic sea state models will be introduced.

docs.title: 11.3.4 Wave spectra
docs.text:
The surface profile of the sea can be considered to be the result of the superposition of a very large number of tiny advancing regular waves of different amplitudes and periods upon one another. This ensemble of waves can, in turn, be described by a frequency spectrum - that is a plot of the spectral density of the square of the deviation of the water surface elevation from mean level against frequency. This spectrum is said to define the sea state, which is usually considered to persist for a period of three hours.

The key parameters of the frequency spectrum are the significant wave height, \({H}_{s}\) , and the frequency corresponding to the peak spectral density, \({f}_{p}\) . The significant wave height is traditionally defined as the average height of the highest one third of waves in a chosen reference period - normally three hours - and corresponds to the height of waves that observers will typically report. The area under the spectrum is equal to the variance of the sea surface elevation, \({\sigma }_{\eta }^{2}\) .

The shape of the frequency spectrum varies according to the fetch and the way wind speeds have varied over the fetch area beforehand. The Pierson-Moskowitz spectrum is a mathematical construct which is considered to provide a good fit to the frequency spectrum of a fully developed sea. In IEC 61400-3, it is specified as:

\[ {S}_{\eta \eta }\left( f\right) = \frac{5}{16}\frac{{H}_{s}^{2}}{f}{\left( \frac{{f}_{p}}{f}\right) }^{4}\exp \left( {-\frac{5}{4}{\left( \frac{{f}_{p}}{f}\right) }^{4}}\right) \tag{11.3} \]

This formulation is based on the assumption that the significant wave height, \({H}_{s}\) , is four times the standard deviation of the sea surface elevation, which is correct for a Rayleigh distribution of wave heights. However, although a Rayleigh distribution of wave heights is strictly generated only by a narrow banded frequency spectrum, it is considered to be a reasonable approximation in the case of real wave spectra.

Fully developed sea states only arise if a wind speed is maintained for long enough over a sufficient fetch. In the majority of situations, either the storm duration or the fetch or both are too small, with the result that the frequency spectra display a more exaggerated peak than the Pierson-Moskowitz (PM) spectrum. The JONSWAP (Joint North Sea Wave Project) spectrum, which was developed from wave measurements near the German island of Sylt, is a variant of the PM spectrum which models this peak enhancement. Essentially the PM spectrum is multiplied by a frequency dependent peak enhancement factor (with a maximum between 1 and 5) and by a normalising factor, which ensures that the area under the JONSWAP spectrum is the same as that under the PM spectrum.

The peak enhancement factor, \({\gamma }^{\alpha }\) , is given in terms of the significant wave height, \({H}_{s}\) , measured in metres, the peak spectral period, \({T}_{p} = 1/{f}_{p}\) seconds, and the frequency, \(f.\gamma = \exp \left\{ {{5.75} - {1.15}{T}_{p}/{H}_{s}^{0.5}}\right\}\) for \({T}_{p}/{H}_{s}^{0.5}\) in the range 3.6 to 5, \(\alpha = \exp \left\{ {-{0.5}{\left( f/{f}_{p} - 1\right) }^{2}/{\sigma }^{2}}\right\} ,\sigma = {0.07}\) for \(f < {f}_{p}\) and \(\sigma = {0.09}\) for \(f > {f}_{p}\) , and the normalising factor is \(1 - {0.287}\ln \gamma .\gamma = 5\) when \({T}_{p}/{H}_{s}^{0.5}\) is less than 3.6 and \(\gamma = 1\) when \({T}_{p}/{H}_{s}^{0.5}\) exceeds 5. It is seen that the JONSWAP spectrum is identical to the PM spectrum when \({T}_{p}/{H}_{s}^{0.5}\) exceeds 5.

The Jonswap and Pierson-Moskowitz spectra are compared for a significant wave height of \(3\mathrm{\;m}\) and peak period of 7 seconds in Figure 11.5.

Figure 11.6 shows an example time history of water surface elevation from a simulation utilising the above Jonswap spectrum.

Figure 11.5 Peirson-Moskowitz and Jonswap spectra for \({H}_{s} = 3\mathrm{\;m}\) and \({T}_{p} = 7\mathrm{{sec}}\)

A description of each wind condition is given in Chapter 5, Section 5.4.2.

The wave conditions are specified as 'normal sea state' or 'normal wave height' in all load cases, apart from load cases 1.6a and 1.6b, for which the 'severe sea state' and the 'severe wave height' respectively apply. These four wave conditions are described in turn below.

docs.title: Normal sea state
docs.text:
IEC 61400-3 defines normal sea states in terms of a stochastic sea state model based on either the Pierson-Moskowitz or Jonswap spectrum as appropriate. For each normal sea state, the significant wave height is to be taken as the expected value at the mean wind speed under consideration, based on analysis of the site-specific metocean database. It is normal to plot the metocean data as a wind-wave scatter diagram, which can be used to derive the expected significant wave height at each wind speed. Typically a two-dimensional wind-wave scatter diagram is presented in the form of a table recording the percentage of time that the mean wind speed and significant wave height lie within different bins in a two-dimensional array. In a three-dimensional scatter diagram, the frequency of occurrence of different peak spectral periods, \({T}_{p}\) , or mean zero-crossing period, \({T}_{z}\) is recorded also. The mean zero-crossing period can be converted to the peak spectral period by means of the relation

\[ {T}_{p} = {T}_{z}\sqrt{\frac{{11} + \gamma }{5 + \gamma }} \]

with gamma as defined in the preceding section.

Data from a two-dimensional scatter diagram for a site designated NL-1 about \({15}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) off Ijmuiden on the Dutch coast is illustrated in Figure 11.7. This shows the frequency of occurrence of different mean wind speeds for each significant wave height at a \({0.5}\mathrm{\;m}\) interval, with reference to a different horizontal axis in each case.

Account should be taken of the range of peak spectral periods, \({T}_{p}\) , encountered and care taken to investigate values of \({T}_{p}\) close to the support structure natural frequency where appropriate.

Marine conditions are essentially the same for all ultimate operational load cases except load case 1.6, and consist of the normal sea state in conjunction with 'normal' currents and water at mean sea level. 'Normal' currents comprise currents induced by the wind, estimated at 1% of the hourly mean wind speed, and breaking wave induced surf currents (if any). The latter may be estimated from the formula \({U}_{bw} = {2s}\sqrt{g{H}_{B}}\) where \(s\) is the sea-floor slope and \({H}_{B}\) the breaking wave height.

Figure 11.7 Data from wind-wave scatter diagram for site NL-1

docs.title: Normal deterministic design wave
docs.text: The height of the normal deterministic design wave is taken as equal to the expected significant wave height at the mean wind speed under consideration.

docs.title: Severe sea state
docs.text:
The IEC 61400-3 severe sea states, which, like the normal sea states, occur during machine operation (load case 1.6a), differ from the normal sea states only in regard to the significant wave height. For each mean wind speed, \(\bar{U}\) , the significant wave height, \({H}_{s,{SSS}}\left( \bar{U}\right)\) is to be taken at a value such that its recurrence period in combination with the mean wind speed is 50 years, based on extrapolation of the site-specific metocean database. The subsection entitled 'Environmental contours' at the end of this section outlines how this extrapolation may be carried out. As with the normal sea state, the most adverse anticipated value of the peak spectral period should be considered.

The other marine conditions for load case 1.6, consist of 'normal' currents and water at any level within the 'normal water level range', which may be taken as the range of astronomic tides.

docs.title: Severe deterministic design wave
docs.text:
IEC 61400-3 load case 1.6b specifies deterministic design waves derived from the significant wave height for the severe sea state (above) at each mean wind speed. The height of the deterministic design wave, or severe wave height, \({H}_{SWH}\left( \bar{U}\right)\) , is the expected height of the extreme wave in the applicable severe sea state. If the wave heights are Rayleigh distributed, then the probability of an individual wave height exceeding \(H\) is

\[ P\left( {h > H}\right) = \exp \left( {-{0.5}{\left( \frac{H/2}{{\sigma }_{\eta }}\right) }^{2}}\right) = \exp \left( {-2{\left( \frac{H}{{H}_{s}}\right) }^{2}}\right) \tag{11.4} \]

and the wave height likely to be exceeded by the highest of \(N\) waves is \({H}_{s}\sqrt{{0.5}\ln N}\) . The expected magnitude of the extreme wave is slightly higher than this at \({H}_{s}\left( {\sqrt{{0.5}\ln N} + {0.2886}/\sqrt{2\ln N}}\right)\) .

For a sea state with mean wave period of 10.8 seconds, there will be 1000 waves in the three-hour reference period, so the extreme wave is likely to exceed \({1.86}{\mathrm{H}}_{s}\) and its expected magnitude is \({1.94}{H}_{\mathrm{s}}\) . However, Annex G of IEC 61400-3 permits the height of the deterministic design wave for each severe sea state to be calculated as \({H}_{SWH}\left( \bar{U}\right) = {1.86}{H}_{s,{SSS}}\left( \overrightarrow{U}\right)\) .

The wave period to be adopted is the value within the range \({11.1}\sqrt{{H}_{s,{SSS}}\left( \bar{U}\right) /g}\) to \({14.3}\sqrt{{H}_{s,{SSS}}\left( \bar{U}\right) /g}\) that results in the highest wave loading.

Load case 1.6b can be omitted if non-linear wave kinematics can be properly modelled in the analysis of load case 1.6a.

docs.title: Environmental contours
docs.text:
One of the load cases representing power production, load case 1.6, is concerned with 50-year return combinations of mean wind speed, \(\bar{U}\) , and significant wave height, \({H}_{s}\) , which, taken together, can be considered as forming an environmental contour in \(\bar{U},{H}_{s}\) space. A method for deriving such a contour using the Inverse First Order Reliability Method (IFORM) is set out in Annex G of IEC 61400-3 and is described in this section.

The probability that a certain combination of mean wind speed and significant wave height will not be exceeded may be written \(F\left( {{H}_{s} \mid \bar{U}}\right) \cdot F\left( \bar{U}\right)\) where \(F\left( \bar{U}\right)\) is the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the mean wind speed and \(F\left( {{H}_{s} \mid \bar{U}}\right)\) is the CDF of the significant wave height conditional on the mean wind speed.

For the 50-year return combination, this probability must equate to \(1 - 1/N\) , where \(N\) is the number of sea states in 50 years - that is, \({50}\left( {365}\right) {24}/3 = {146},{000}\) for a three-hour sea state duration.

The environmental contour may be derived by utilising a transformation from mean wind speed and significant wave height to two uncorrelated normally distributed variables, \({U}_{1}\) and \({U}_{2}\) , so that

\[ F\left( \bar{U}\right) = \Phi \left( {U}_{1}\right) \;\text{ and }\;F\left( {{H}_{S} \mid \bar{U}}\right) = \Phi \left( {U}_{2}\right) \tag{11.5} \] \[ \text{ where }\Phi \left( U\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}{\int }_{-\infty }^{U}\exp \left\lbrack {-{u}^{2}/2}\right\rbrack {du} \tag{11.6} \]

The joint probability density function (pdf) of the normally distributed variables \({U}_{1}\) and \({U}_{2}\) is

\[ p\left( {{U}_{1},{U}_{2}}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\exp \left\lbrack {-\frac{{U}_{1}^{2}}{2}}\right\rbrack \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi }}\exp \left\lbrack {-\frac{{U}_{2}^{2}}{2}}\right\rbrack = \frac{1}{2\pi }\exp \left\lbrack {-\frac{{U}_{1}^{2} + {U}_{2}^{2}}{2}}\right\rbrack \tag{11.7} \]

so the joint pdf is axi-symmetric about the origin and points in \({U}_{1},{U}_{2}\) space lying at the same radius from the origin have the same probability density. The joint pdf is illustrated in Figure 11.8.

Figure 11.8 Joint probability density of two uncorrelated normally distributed variables

Figure 11.9 Circle of radius \(\beta\) in \({U}_{1} \cdot {U}_{2}\) space, representing environmental contour

Clearly the \(N\) year return wind speed, irrespective of significant wave height, is that for which \(F\left( \bar{U}\right) = \Phi \left( {U}_{1}\right) = 1 - 1/N\) , that is, for which \({U}_{1} = {\Phi }^{-1}\left( {1 - 1/N}\right)\) . In \({U}_{1},{U}_{2}\) space, the probability that the wind exceeds the \(N\) year return value is represented by the probability that the point \({U}_{1},{U}_{2}\) lies to the right of the line ABC in Figure 11.9, with \(\beta\) set equal to \({\Phi }^{-1}\left( {1 - 1/N}\right)\) .

Given that the volume under the joint probability density function surface (Figure 11.8) lying beyond any tangent to the circle radius \(\beta\) is the same, it follows that the probability that a point \({U}_{1},{U}_{2}\) lies beyond the tangent DEF is the same as the probability that a point \({U}_{1},{U}_{2}\) lies beyond the tangent ABC - that is, \(1/N\) . Thus, the circle radius \(\beta\) is the internal envelope of a family of tangents such that the probability of \({U}_{1},{U}_{2}\) lying outside each one is \(1/N\) . In this sense, it represents the \(N\) -year environmental contour transformed into two dimensional normal space. Note that the portions of the circle for which \({U}_{1}\) or \({U}_{2}\) is negative represent \(N\) -year return minimum values in each case.

A procedure for the practical application of the method to metocean data in the form of a mean wind speed/significant wave height scatter diagram is as follows:

  1. (a) Using the scatter diagram, calculate the non-exceedance probability, \(F\left( \bar{U}\right)\) , associated with the mean wind speed, \(\bar{U}\) , of a particular wind speed bin.

(b) Calculate the corresponding value of the normally distributed variable \({U}_{1} = {\Phi }^{-1}\left( {F\left( \bar{U}\right) }\right) .\)

(c) Calculate \({U}_{2} = \sqrt{{\beta }^{2} - {U}_{1}^{2}}\) . (The negative root corresponds to the minimum value of \({H}_{s}\) .)

(d) Calculate the 50 year return significant wave height conditional on \(\bar{U}\) as

\[ {H}_{s,{SSS}}\left( \bar{U}\right) = {\bar{H}}_{s}\left( \bar{U}\right) + {U}_{2}{\sigma }_{{H}_{S}}\left( \bar{U}\right) \]

where \({\bar{H}}_{s}\left( \bar{U}\right)\) and \({\sigma }_{{H}_{S}}\left( \bar{U}\right)\) are the mean and standard deviation of the significant wave height conditional on \(\bar{U}\) extracted from the scatter diagram, respectively.

  1. Repeat step 1. for the other wind speed bins.

  2. Plot environmental contour linking the points \({H}_{s,{SSS}}\left( \bar{U}\right) ,\bar{U}\) .

Note that in the above procedure, it is assumed that the significant wave heights conditional on \(\bar{U}\) are normally distributed, which may not necessarily be consistent with the data. It is more conservative to assume that the significant wave heights are log-normally distributed. Whichever model is adopted, goodness of fit tests - visual and/or statistical - should be carried out to confirm its suitability.

An example of 50-year return environmental contours derived from the scatter diagram for the NL-1 site (see Figure 11.7) is given in Figure 11.10. One contour is based on a normal distribution of significant wave heights conditional on \(\bar{U}\) and the other is based on a lognormal distribution.

Figure 11.10 50-year significant wave height against mean wind speed environmental contours derived from site NL-1 scatter diagram

docs.title: 11.3.6 Ultimate loads: non-operational load cases and accompanying wave climates
docs.text:
An overview of the IEC 61400-3 ultimate load cases for non-operational loading is given in Table 11.3, which identifies the equivalent onshore load case in IEC 61400-1 in each case.

It is seen that for each of the four IEC 61400-1 load cases applicable onshore, IEC 61400-3 specifies two or three sub load cases for use offshore, which are distinguished by suffices \(a, b\) and \(c\) . These differ as follows:

  • Suffix \(a\) load cases specify the extreme turbulent wind in conjunction with the extreme stochastic sea state.

Table 11.3 Ultimate non-operational load cases

M/c stateLoad case no.Equiv LC on landWind conditionsWind speedWave conditionsWater LevelGrid, yaw and fault statusLoad case typeParked (standing still or idling)6.1a6.150-yr EWM turbulent${k}_{1}{U}_{ref}$50-yr extreme sea state ${H}_{s} = \; {k}_{2}{H}_{s50}$Extreme rangeNoneN6.1b6.150-yr EWM steady${U}_{e50}$50-yr reduced wave height $H = \sim {0.7}{H}_{50}$Extreme rangeNoneN6.1cNone50-yr RWM steady0.786 ✘ ${U}_{e50}$50-yr extreme wave height $H = {H}_{50}$Extreme rangeNoneN6.2a6.250-yr EWM turbulent${k}_{1}{U}_{ref}$50-yr extreme sea state ${H}_{s} = \; {k}_{2}{H}_{s50}$Extreme rangeGrid loss, ${180}^{ \circ }$ yawA6.2b6.250-yr EWM steady${U}_{e50}$50 yr Reduced wave height $H = \sim {0.7}{H}_{50}$Extreme rangeGrid loss, ${180}^{ \circ }$ yawA6.3a6.31-yr EWM turbulent0.8 ✘ ${k}_{1}{U}_{ref}$1-yr extreme sea state ${H}_{s} = {k}_{2} \; {H}_{s1}$Normal rangeExtreme yaw $\left( {20}^{ \circ }\right)$N6.3b6.31-yr EWM steady${U}_{e1}$1-yr reduced wave height $H = \sim {0.7}{H}_{1}$Normal rangeExtreme yaw $\left( {30}^{ \circ }\right)$NParked with fault condition7.1a7.11-yr EWM turbulent${0.8} \times \; {k}_{1}{U}_{ref}$1-yr extreme sea state ${H}_{s} = {k}_{2} \; {H}_{s1}$Normal rangeFault conditionA7.1b7.11-yr EWM steady${U}_{e1}$1-yr reduced wave height $H = \sim {0.7}{H}_{1}$Normal rangeFault conditionA7.1cNone1-yr RWM steady0.786 $\times \; {U}_{e1}$1-yr extreme wave height $H = {H}_{1}$Normal rangeFault conditionA

EWM and RWM stand for extreme wind speed model and reduced wind speed model respectively.

  • Suffix \(b\) load cases specify the extreme steady wind in conjunction with the ’reduced’ deterministic design wave ( \({0.7} \times\) height of extreme deterministic design wave).

  • Suffix \(c\) load cases specify the ’reduced’ steady wind ( \({1.1}/{1.4} \times\) extreme steady wind) in conjunction with the extreme deterministic design wave.

The designer is given the option of considering either the stochastic load case \(a\) or deterministic cases \(b\) and \(c\) (where included). The wind and wave/sea state return periods are 50 years for 'fault-free' load cases 6.1 and 6.2 and one year for load cases 6.3 and 7.1, which involve extreme yaw and a machine fault respectively. Note that the grid loss load case 6.2 can include a yaw error of up to \({180}^{ \circ }\) , unless six hours back-up power supply is provided for the control and yaw system.

Note that in the suffix \(a\) load cases, it is assumed that the extreme stochastic sea state occurs at the same time as the extreme turbulent wind.

The suffix \(b\) and \(c\) load cases simplify the investigation of non-linear wave loading, which is computationally demanding for the multiple superposed linear waves forming the stochastic sea state of the suffix \(a\) load case. Unfortunately, the suffix \(b\) and \(c\) load cases cannot capture the dynamic response of the turbine structure to the turbulent wind, although Annex D of the standard describes how the steady wind speed should be increased above the design value to correct for this. Two deterministic load cases are required, because the possibility of the extreme gust and the extreme wave loadings occurring simultaneously is assumed to be negligible and instances of dominant wind and dominant wave loading both have to be catered for. The chosen reduction factors of 0.7 for wave height in the suffix \(b\) load cases and \({1.1}/{1.4}\left( { = {0.79}}\right)\) for wind speed in the suffix \(c\) load cases are based on work by Tarp-Johansen (2005). This showed that, if the wind and wave loading are treated as Gaussian quantities and the wave loading is drag-dominated, a reduction factor of \(\sqrt{0.35} = {0.59}\) for wave height in the suffix \(b\) dominant wind load cases and a reduction factor of \(\sqrt{0.65} = {0.81}\) for wind speed in the suffix \(c\) dominant wave load cases result in the best fit of those load cases to the total loading, regardless of the relative wind and wave load magnitudes.

Consideration of the effect of possible misalignment between wind and wave directions is required for all the non-operational load cases.

docs.title: Extreme sea state
docs.text:
The stochastic sea state model for the IEC 61400-3 extreme sea state is the same as for the normal sea state in Section 11.2.5, but the significant wave heights to be considered are those with a 50 year or one year return period, depending on the load case. These may be determined by extrapolation based on the tail of the long-term distribution of significant wave heights. As with the normal sea state, the most adverse anticipated value of the peak spectral period is to be considered.

The other marine conditions consist of extreme currents (including currents generated by tides and storm surges) and water level range with the same recurrence period as the significant wave height combined with storm surge.

As the extreme wind speed \({U}_{\text{ ref }}\) is defined as the ten-minute mean, and the reference period for the significant wave height is normally three hours, a common averaging period for both parameters needs to be adopted for the simulations of extreme wind and wave loading in the suffix \(a\) load cases. The standard uses a common averaging period of one hour, defining the hourly mean wind speed as the ten-minute mean multiplied by a factor, \({k}_{1}\) , of 0.95 and the one hour value of the turbulence standard deviation as the ten-minute value plus \({0.2}\mathrm{\;m}/\mathrm{s}\) . Similarly, the significant wave height for a three-hour reference period is multiplied by the factor, \({k}_{2}\) , of 1.09 to convert it to the value appropriate to the shorter, one-hour reference period.

Normally at least six one-hour simulations are required, but shorter simulations are acceptable if it can be demonstrated that this will not reduce the extreme response - for example, by the use of the 'constrained wave' described in Section 11.3.10.

docs.title: Extreme deterministic design wave
docs.text:
Two extreme deterministic design waves are specified - with return periods of 50 years and one year.

If the wave heights in the extreme sea states are Rayleigh distributed, then the wave height expected to be exceeded by the highest of \(N\) waves is \({H}_{s}\sqrt{{0.5}\ln N}\) . Taking \(N = {1000}\) as before results in an extreme wave height with 50-year and one-year return periods of \({H}_{50} = {1.86}{H}_{s50}\) and \({H}_{1} = {1.86}{H}_{s1}\) respectively.

docs.title: Modification of wave climate in shallow water
docs.text: Waves begin to break when the wave height reaches \({78}\%\) of the mean water depth, so the upper tail of the Rayleigh distribution of wave heights becomes curtailed as deep sea waves advance into shallower water, leading to conservatism in the use of the \({1.86}{\mathrm{H}}_{s}\) formula for the wave height exceeded by the largest of 1000 waves. Battjes and Groeneddijk (2000) have developed a model for calculating the modified distribution of wave heights for waves propagating over a uniformly sloping seabed - see Annex C of IEC-61400-3. The model depends on the availability of measured site-specific wave data and is applicable provided the wave direction is within \({30}^{ \circ }\) of the direction of steepest seabed slope.

docs.title: 11.3.7 Fatigue loads
docs.text:
An overview of the IEC 61400-3 fatigue load cases - operational and non-operational - is given in Table 11.4, which identifies the equivalent onshore load case in IEC 61400-1 in each case.

The wind conditions and water levels denoted by the acronyms in the table above are as follows:

NTM Normal turbulence model

NWP Normal wind profile (following a power law with exponent of 0.14), without turbulence

NSS Normal sea state

NWLR Normal water level range

MSL Mean Sea Level

Sea currents are ignored.

A range of significant wave heights and wave periods should be considered at each wind speed, with the duration of each combination of wind speed and sea state extracted from a site specific three-dimensional scatter diagram. In particular \({T}_{p}\) values corresponding to the natural frequency of the support structure should be investigated. However, it is preferable to avoid a very large number of simulations, so it is advantageous to lump load cases together

Table 11.4 Fatigue load cases

M/c stateLoad case no.Equiv LC on landWind conditionsWind speedWave conditionsWater levelGrid, yaw and fault statusPower production1.21.2NTMCut-in - Cut-outNSS Joint prob. distribution of ${H}_{s},{T}_{p},\bar{U}$NWLR or ≥MSLNonePower production with fault2.42.4NTMCut-in - Cut-outNormal sea state i.e. ${H}_{s} = \; E\left\lbrack {{H}_{s} \mid \bar{U}}\right\rbrack$NWLR or ≥MSLFault conditionStart-up3.13.1NWPCut-in - Cut-outNormal Sea State i.e. ${H}_{s} = \; E\left\lbrack {{H}_{s} \mid \bar{U}}\right\rbrack$NWLR or ≥MSLNoneNormal shut down4.14.1NWPCut-in - Cut-outNormal sea state i.e. ${H}_{s} = \; E\left\lbrack {{H}_{s} \mid \bar{U}}\right\rbrack$NWLR or ≥MSLNoneParked6.46.4NTM$< {0.7}{U}_{ref}$NSS joint prob. distribution of ${H}_{s},{T}_{p},\bar{U}$NWLR or ≥MSLNoneParked with fault condition7.2NoneNTM$< {0.56}{U}_{ref}$NSS joint prob. distribution of ${H}_{s},{T}_{p},\bar{U}$NWLR or ≥MSLFault condition

if possible. The errors due to coarsening the wave height and wave period bins can be reduced if the 'damage equivalent mean wave height' and 'damage equivalent mean period' are calculated for each bin. The former is determined as

\[ {H}_{s} = {\left( \frac{1}{N}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{N}{H}_{{s}_{i}}^{m}\right) }^{\frac{1}{m}} \]

where \(m\) is the inverse slope of the \(S - N\) curve, and the latter is taken as the reciprocal of the mean wave frequency. In a case study, Evans (2005) showed that, for a wind speed bin width of \(2\mathrm{\;m}/\mathrm{s}\) , the error in damage equivalent load resulting from a move from \({0.5}\mathrm{\;m}\) wave height and \({0.5}\mathrm{\;s}\) wave period bin widths to a single wave height/wave period bin with this approach was only a few per cent.

IEC 61400-3 specifies two fatigue load cases for machines that are parked or idling - one without and the other with a fault condition. The latter is absent from IEC 61400-1, but is considered necessary offshore because of the potentially much longer machine down-times and the large reduction in aerodynamic damping when the turbine is shut down.

The maximum wind speed to be considered for fatigue loading on a parked turbine in the absence of a fault (DLC 6.4) is \({0.7}{U}_{ref}\) - a value likely to be exceeded for 0.6 hour per year.

However, for fatigue loading on a parked turbine with a fault condition (DLC 7.2), the upper wind speed to be considered is only \({0.56}{U}_{ref}\) , which is likely to be exceeded for 19 hours per year. No guidance is given on the likely total turbine down time corresponding to DLC 7.2 and clearly this needs to be predicted with great care.

docs.title: 11.3.8 Wave theories
docs.text:
Several wave theories exist to describe the fluid motion within regular, periodic, two-dimensional waves, but only three are routinely used for the calculation of loads on offshore structures - Airy, Stokes and Dean's Stream Function Theories.

Airy wave theory is linear and, therefore, allows the water particle kinematics of a real sea state, consisting of a multitude of small waves of varying frequencies and wave lengths, to be modelled by superposition. However, as wave height increases in relation to water depth or wave-length, Airy theory becomes less accurate and non-linear theories such as Stokes and Dean's Stream Function have to be employed instead. However, because of their nonlinearity, these theories can only be applied to single, regular wave trains. Figure 11.11 shows which theories are applicable for different relationships between wave height, water depth and wave period.

Figure 11.11 Regular wave theory selection diagram: log scales. Barltrop et al., 1990. Reproduced under the Open Government License v1.0

It is apparent from Figure 11.11 that Dean's Stream Function theory can be used for all but near breaking waves. In view of this, and the relative complexity of Stokes Wave Theory, the latter is not discussed further and this section concentrates on the other two theories.

docs.title: Airy wave theory
docs.text:
The fluid motion within regular, periodic two-dimensional waves must satisfy the Laplace equation, \({\nabla }^{2}\phi \left( {x, z, t}\right) = 0\) , where \(\phi\) is the velocity potential, defined so that horizontal and vertical particle velocities are given by \(u = - \partial \phi /\partial x\) and \(w = - \partial \phi /\partial z\) respectively. \(x\) is the horizontal co-ordinate parallel to the direction of wave motion and \(z\) is the vertical co-ordinate measured upwards with respect to mean water level, as shown in Figure 11.12.

The fluid motion must also satisfy five boundary conditions as follows:

  1. Zero flow vertical particle velocity, \(w\) , at the seabed, which is assumed horizontal.

  2. Zero flow perpendicular to the free surface.

  3. The unsteady form of the Bernouilli equation at the free surface.

  4. The periodic boundary condition in time \(- \phi \left( {x, z, t}\right) = \phi \left( {x, z, t + T}\right)\) , where \(T\) is the wave period.

  5. The periodic boundary condition in space \(- \phi \left( {x, z, t}\right) = \phi \left( {x + L, z, t}\right)\) , where \(L\) is the wave length.

Condition (2) is expressed as:

\[ w = \frac{\partial \eta }{\partial t} + u\frac{\partial \eta }{\partial x} \tag{11.8} \]

where \(\eta\) is the water surface elevation above the mean and \(u\) is the horizontal water particle velocity. The atmospheric pressure acting on the free surface of the water is treated as constant, so the unsteady form of the Bernouilli equation in condition (3) becomes:

\[ - \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial t} + \frac{{u}^{2} + {w}^{2}}{2} + {gz} = C\left( t\right) \tag{11.9} \]

Figure 11.12 Parameter definitions and co-ordinates for regular, periodic, two-dimensional waves

Figure 11.13 Velocity potential contours for Airy wave theory

According to Airy wave theory, the velocity potential at any point in the water is:

\[ \phi = - \frac{Hg}{2\omega }\frac{\cosh k\left( {z + d}\right) }{\cosh {kd}}\sin \left( {{kx} - {\omega t}}\right) \tag{11.10} \]

where \(H\) is the wave height, \(d\) is the mean water depth, \(k = {2\pi }/L\) and \(\omega = {2\pi }/T\) . Figure 11.13 shows the corresponding velocity potential contours over a full wave length for the case of a \({15}\mathrm{\;m}\) water depth and \({80}\mathrm{\;m}\) wave length. Note that the contours are shown as extending only up to still water level, as Airy wave theory only approaches 100% accuracy as the wave height becomes vanishingly small. Assuming the waves are moving from left to right, the maximum velocity potential is at the water surface at the right hand quarter point.

The equation for velocity potential satisfies conditions (1), (4) and (5) above exactly, but only satisfies 'linearised' versions of Equations 11.8 and 11.9.

The 'linearised' version of Equation 11.9 is obtained by expanding the left hand side of the equation with respect to the value at \(z = 0\) using a truncated Taylor’s series to give.

\[ {\left( -\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial t} + \frac{{u}^{2} + {w}^{2}}{2} + gz\right) }_{z = \eta } = {\left( -\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial t} + \frac{{u}^{2} + {w}^{2}}{2} + gz\right) }_{z = 0} \] \[ + \eta {\left( -\frac{{\partial }^{2}\phi }{\partial t\partial z} + \frac{\partial }{\partial z}\left( \frac{{u}^{2} + {w}^{2}}{2}\right) + g\right) }_{z = 0} + \cdots . = C\left( t\right) \]

(11.11)

Then, assuming all first order terms are small, all second order terms are very small, and can be neglected, giving

\[ {\left( -\frac{\partial \phi }{\partial t}\right) }_{z = 0} + {\eta g} = C\left( t\right) \;\text{ or }\;\eta = \frac{1}{g}{\left( \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial t}\right) }_{z = 0} + \frac{1}{g}C\left( t\right) \tag{11.12} \]

Substituting Equation 11.10 in Equation 11.12 and noting that the spatial and temporal means of the water surface elevation are defined as zero yields \(C\left( t\right) = 0\) and

\[ \eta = \frac{H}{2}\cos \left( {{kx} - {\omega t}}\right) \tag{11.13} \]

Application of a similar procedure to Equation 11.8 yields \(w = \partial \eta /\partial t\) at \(z = 0\) , and substitution of

\[ w = - {\left( \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial z}\right) }_{z = 0} = \frac{Hgk}{2\omega }\frac{\sinh {kd}}{\cosh {kd}}\sin \left( {{kx} - {\omega t}}\right) \tag{11.14} \]

and \({\left( \partial \eta /\partial t\right) }_{z = 0} = \left( {H/2}\right) \omega \sin \left( {{kx} - {\omega t}}\right)\) results in

\[ L = \frac{g{T}^{2}}{2\pi }\tanh {kd} \tag{11.15} \]

The horizontal and vertical particle velocities at any depth, \(u\) and \(w\) , are given by

\[ u = - \left( \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial x}\right) = \frac{Hgk}{2\omega }\frac{\cosh k\left( {z + d}\right) }{\cosh {kd}}\cos \left( {{kx} - {\omega t}}\right) = \frac{H\omega }{2}\frac{\cosh k\left( {z + d}\right) }{\sinh {kd}}\cos \left( {{kx} - {\omega t}}\right) \]

(11.16)

\[ w = - \left( \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial z}\right) = \frac{Hgk}{2\omega }\frac{\sinh k\left( {z + d}\right) }{\cosh {kd}}\sin \left( {{kx} - {\omega t}}\right) = \frac{H\omega }{2}\frac{\sinh k\left( {z + d}\right) }{\sinh {kd}}\sin \left( {{kx} - {\omega t}}\right) \]

(11.17)

The particle displacements can be obtained by integrating the above expressions. The water particles follow elliptical orbits with the major axis horizontal, as shown in Figure 11.12.

Figure 11.14 shows the accuracy of Airy wave theory in predicting the horizontal particle velocity at the wave crest by comparison with the more accurate Dean/Stokes \({5}^{\text{ th }}\) theories for different \(H/g{T}^{2}\) and \(d/g{T}^{2}\) ratios. This Figure is taken from Dynamics of Fixed Marine Structures by Barltrop and Adams (1991), which contains similar Figures applicable to the prediction accuracy for other parameters.

docs.title: Dean's stream function theory
docs.text:
Dean's stream function theory (Dean and Dalrymple, 1984) is effectively an extension of Airy wave theory achieved by the addition of a series of harmonic terms to the expression for velocity potential, which enable the theory to satisfy the boundary conditions at the free surface (Equations 11.8 and 11.9) without the need for 'linearisation'. However, rather than use the velocity potential, the theory is developed with reference to the parameter known as the stream function, which is now introduced.

The paths followed by water particles within the waves are termed streamlines, along each of which the stream function parameter has a constant value. The stream function is defined such that its gradient perpendicular to the streamlines is proportional to the local particle velocity, so that

\[ u = - \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial z}\;\text{ and }\;w = \frac{\partial \psi }{\partial x} \tag{11.18} \]

Figure 11.14 Horizontal particle velocity at the wave crest: Airy theory as % of theory shown in Figure 11.11. Barltrop et al., 1990. Reproduced under the Open Government License v1.0

For Airy wave theory, the stream function is

\[ \psi = - \frac{Hg}{2\omega }\frac{\sinh k\left( {z + d}\right) }{\cosh {kd}}\cos \left( {{kx} - {\omega t}}\right) \tag{11.19} \]

The corresponding streamlines are shown over a full wave length in Figure 11.15, for the case of a \({15}\mathrm{\;m}\) water depth and \({80}\mathrm{\;m}\) wave length.

The streamlines in Equation 11.19 and Figure 11.15 are defined with respect to a fixed frame of reference. However, it is perfectly possible to define them with respect to a moving frame of reference which travels at the same speed as the wave crests and troughs - that is, with celerity \(C = L/T\) . Then the Airy wave theory stream function becomes

\[ \overline{\psi } = {Cz} - \frac{Hg}{2\omega }\frac{\sinh k\left( {z + d}\right) }{\cosh {kd}}\cos \left( {kx}\right) \tag{11.20} \]

Figure 11.15 Streamlines for Airy wave theory with the frame of reference fixed. Note that, as with the figure illustrating the velocity potential contours, the streamlines are shown as only extending up to still water level, because Airy wave theory only approaches 100% accuracy as the wave height becomes vanishingly small

which has the advantage of being invariant with time. The streamlines corresponding to the moving frame of reference are shown over a full wave length in Figure 11.16, for the same case as above. However, for clarity a relatively large wave height of \(4\mathrm{\;m}\) is chosen, for which the Airy solution is inaccurate.

Dean's stream function is defined with respect to the same moving frame of reference, and consists of a harmonic series of terms as follows:

\[ \overline{\psi } = {Cz} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{N}{X}_{n}\sinh {nk}\left( {z + d}\right) \cos \left( {nkx}\right) \tag{11.21} \]

For \(N = 1\) , Equation 11.21 equates to Equation 11.20, so

\[ {X}_{1} = - \frac{Hg}{{2\omega }\cosh {kd}} \tag{11.22} \]

Figure 11.16 Streamlines for Airy wave theory with frame of reference moving with the wave train

The corresponding water particle velocities are:

\[ u = - \frac{\partial \overline{\psi }}{\partial z} = - C - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{N}{nk}{X}_{n}\cosh {nk}\left( {z + d}\right) \cos \left( {nkx}\right) \tag{11.23} \] \[ w = \frac{\partial \overline{\psi }}{\partial x} = - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{N}{nk}{X}_{n}\sinh {nk}\left( {z + d}\right) \sin \left( {nkx}\right) \tag{11.24} \]

The number of terms, \(N\) , required increases as the height of the waves approaches the breaking limit. A solution using \(N\) terms is described as \(N\) th order. Substituting \(z = \eta\) at the free surface in Equation 11.21 gives:

\[ \eta = \frac{{\overline{\psi }}_{0}}{C} - \frac{1}{C}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{N}{X}_{n}\sinh {nk}\left( {\eta + d}\right) \cos \left( {nkx}\right) ) \tag{11.25} \]

Given that the spatial average of the water surface elevation, \(\eta\) , is zero by definition, we have

\[ {\overline{\psi }}_{0} = \frac{1}{L}{\int }_{0}^{L}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{n = 1}}^{N}{X}_{n}\sinh {nk}\left( {\eta + d}\right) \cos \left( {nkx}\right) {dx} \tag{11.26} \]

(The expression on the right hand side of this equation is non-zero by virtue of the variable weighting of \(\cos \left( {nkx}\right)\) by the hyperbolic factor, \(\sinh {nk}\left( {\eta + d}\right)\) .)

The boundary conditions to be satisfied are as follows:

  1. Zero flow vertical particle velocity, \(w\) , at the seabed, which is assumed horizontal.

  2. Zero flow perpendicular to the free surface.

  3. The steady form of the Bernouilli equation at the free surface.

  4. The periodic boundary condition in space \(\overline{\Psi }\left( {x, z}\right) = \overline{\Psi }\left( {x + L, z}\right)\) , where \(L\) is the wave length.

Equations 11.24 and 11.21 satisfy condition (1) and (4) respectively, while condition (2) is satisfied because the free surface is a streamline.

The steady form of the Bernoulli equation at the free surface (condition (3)) is:

\[ \left( \frac{{u}^{2} + {w}^{2}}{2}\right) + {g\eta } = K \tag{11.27} \]

If the wave length, the mean water depth and the wave height, \(H\) , are the known quantities, the solution to the problem resolves itself into finding of a set of values of the \({X}_{n}\) coefficients combined with a value of celerity, \(C\) , such that Equation 11.27 is satisfied as closely as possible at all points along the wave profile subject to the condition \({\eta }_{\max } - {\eta }_{\min } = H\) . The following steps enable a low order solution to be obtained on a spreadsheet:

  1. Set \({X}_{2},{X}_{3}\ldots {X}_{N}\) all equal to zero.

  2. Set \(C = \sqrt{\left( {g/k}\right) \tanh {kd}}\) , the value according to Airy wave theory.

  3. Set \({X}_{1}\) somewhat smaller than given by Equation (11.22) - say \({X}_{1} = \; - {0.8}\mathrm{{Hg}}/\left( {{2\omega }\cosh {kd}}\right)\) .

  4. Calculate the water level profile at \(M\) equally spaced points over a half wave length using repeated iterations of Equations 11.25 and 11.26.

  5. Using Equation 11.27, calculate values of \({K}_{1},{K}_{2},\ldots {K}_{m},\ldots {K}_{M}\) at these \(M\) points.

  6. Calculate the summation \(\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m = 1}}^{M}{\left( {K}_{m} - \bar{K}\right) }^{2}\) , where \(\bar{K} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m = 1}}^{M}{K}_{m}/M\) .

  7. Minimise the above summation with respect to \({X}_{1}\) and \(C\) , subject to the condition \({\eta }_{\max } - {\eta }_{\min } = H\) , to obtain new values of \({X}_{1}\) and \(C\) .

  8. Repeat steps 4-7 with \({X}_{2}\) allowed to vary as well.

  9. Repeat steps 4-7 with \({X}_{2}\) and \({X}_{3}\) allowed to vary as well.

  10. Etc., etc.

Streamlines derived from a fifth order solution using this method with an \(M\) of 40 are shown over a half wave length in Figure 11.17, for the case of a \({15}\mathrm{\;m}\) water depth, \({100}\mathrm{\;m}\) wave length and \({10}\mathrm{\;m}\) wave height. It is evident that the wave profile is far from sinusoidal, with a narrow crest and a broad trough, so that the crest is much higher above mean sea level than the trough is below it.

Horizontal particle velocities may be calculated from the stream function using Equation 11.23. The profiles of horizontal particle velocities relative to a fixed frame of reference beneath the crest and beneath the trough are shown in Figure 11.18 for the above example.

Figure 11.17 Streamlines for Dean stream function wave theory with moving frame of reference

Figure 11.18 Horizontal particle velocity profiles below wave crest and trough. Note the high horizontal particle velocity at the crest, which approaches the wave celerity

A useful on-line resource providing the Dean stream function theory coefficients and the wave profile for user input wave parameters is to be found at http://www.coastal.udel.edu/faculty/rad/streamless.html at the time of writing.

docs.title: 11.3.9 Wave loading on support structure
docs.text: The wave loading on immersed structures depends on their size, shape and surface roughness. For elements that are small compared with the wavelength, the disturbance to wave behaviour caused by the structure can be ignored and the loading based on the undisturbed wave kinematics, using Morison's equation. However, for larger elements, it is necessary to take account of the way the wave pattern is modified.
