docs.title: 11.7 Environmental assessment of offshore wind farms
docs.text:
Offshore wind farms extend over large areas of often environmentally important, shallow waters and have the potential to make a considerable impact on the marine environment. As with any large onshore wind farm project, an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is necessary before an application for consent to construct and operate an offshore wind farm is submitted. In Europe the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (97/11/EC, 1997) requires an EIA to be undertaken and an Environmental Statement must be submitted with any proposal to develop an offshore wind farm. Detailed guidance on how this requirement is translated into UK legislation is given in CEFAS (2004).

The EIA assesses the environmental impacts of the project at all stages of construction, operation and de-commissioning. It considers measures that can be adopted for avoiding any undesirable impacts or, if this is not possible, mitigating them. The primary readership of the Environmental Statement is the authorities who must give permission for the project to proceed but also the various stakeholders with an interest in the marine environment. Coastal areas are used for a range of purposes, for example fishing, mineral extraction, shipping or recreation, and there are likely to be many groups with a keen interest in any proposed offshore wind farm development. Best practice on how the consultation should be managed is described in BWEA (2002).

The contents of any Environmental Statement are described in 97/11/EC as including a description of the project and the measures proposed to avoid and mitigate significant adverse effects. It will include the data necessary to identify and assess the main effects which the project is likely to have on the environment and an outline of the main alternatives studied by the project developer. The choices made in the development of the project must be justified taking into account the environmental effects. Both a comprehensive technical document and a shorter non-technical summary are required. Before detailed work is undertaken, including data collection and surveys, it is usual to agree a scoping report with the permitting authority that defines the extent of the investigations of the EIA.

In addition to the EIA required for an individual wind farm project, Strategic Environmental Assessments (SEA) are undertaken by national or regional governments to identify those areas where offshore wind farm development is appropriate and to identify where particular emphasis is required in the individual project EIAs (EWEA, 2009; DECC, 2009). For example, the SEA for the second round of UK offshore wind farm development identified three Strategic Areas; Greater Wash, Thames Estuary and off North-West England. It established a number of important principles. Larger wind farms (around 1000 MW) were preferred to smaller inshore projects. Wind turbines were excluded from a coastal strip of \(8\mathrm{\;{km}}\) that was extended to \({13}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) in areas of particular landscape sensitivity. Also, wind turbines were not to be installed in areas of less than \({10}\mathrm{\;m}\) water depth due to the particular value of the natural environment of these shallow areas in terms of bird habitat, visual impact and use for recreation and inshore fishing. All three areas were close to electrical load centres and had good access to the electrical transmission system. After publication of the SEA, expressions of interest were received for the development of 7.2 GW of offshore wind energy.

EIAs for offshore wind farms start with a description of the complete proposed development and this will include the wind turbines, their layout and foundations, the array cabling, the offshore substation, the submarine transmission cable to shore, the land cable and any additional works for the land substation. Considerable work is undertaken to gather data of the project area including surveys of the seabed, marine biology, birds and mammals, fish resources, marine traffic, the intertidal area where the power cables come ashore, and archaeology. A baseline survey for landscape and seascape visual assessment is also undertaken. It is common for a period of post-construction and commissioning environmental monitoring to be required.

Particular environmental impacts that need to be considered include:

  • Coastal and sedimentary processes - sediment transport, scouring.

  • Wave and tidal environment.

  • Water quality - turbidity.

  • Benthos - the flora and fauna of the seabed.

  • Fish resources - migration patterns, nursery areas.

  • Commercial fisheries.

  • Marine navigation.

  • Archaeology.

  • Marine mammals - distribution, disturbance, displacement impacts of noise and vibration.

  • Birds - distribution, disturbance, displacement, mortality.

  • Designated areas (i.e. defined areas considered to be of environmental importance where particular protection policies are in place).

As with onshore wind farms, changes to the landscape and visual impact are likely to be of concern and a possible cause of objections to the wind farm development. DTI, 2005 provides detailed guidance on how Seascape and Visual Impact Assessment (SVIA) of offshore wind energy developments may be undertaken. The extent of the potential visibility of the development is described using Zones of Theoretical Visual influence (ZTV). This technique defines the areas from which one or more wind turbines, or parts of a wind turbine, are visible taking into account topography and curvature of the earth but not making any allowance for atmospheric conditions. Thus, a ZTV indicates the furthest possible extent of visibility. In order to take account of differing atmospheric and lighting conditions, the visual impact of the development is illustrated using wireframes and photomontages from viewpoints that have been agreed during the scoping phase. For large wind farms three-dimensional modelling and video-montages are used increasingly. For wind farms greater than \({24}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) from shore visual impacts are likely to be minor. The SVIA identifies the features of the existing seascape and the changes that the wind farm development would make to its visual character. The judgement is based on an assessment of receptor sensitivity and the capacity of the seascape to accommodate change. From the land, local residents are considered to be the most sensitive receptors with industrial activities, for example ports, the least sensitive. Similarly, out to sea, recreational boating has high sensitivity receptors while oil and gas rigs are less sensitive. The capacity of the seascape to accommodate change is evaluated considering the overall quality and sensitivity of the seascape to the wind farm as well as the value attached to the seascape. DTI, 2005 gives guidance on how these judgements can be made and the results recorded.

Noise, particularly during construction, has been an issue for some offshore wind farms that are close to shore. Installations of mono-pile foundations can be particularly noisy and restrictions may be placed on hours of work. The noise transmitted under water during piling operations can be very loud \(\left( {{200}\mathrm{\;{dB}}\text{ at }1\mathrm{\;m}}\right)\) and it is common practice to use a soft-start to piling operations so that fish and marine mammals leave the area.

Local scour around the turbine and substation foundations and cable routes is a common concern and scour protection (e.g. using rock dumping) may be required. This alters the surface of the seabed and can lead to changes in the benthic flora and fauna.

Ships and boats often use simple, low cost pulsed radar rather than the more sophisticated equipment commonly found in aviation radars that use the Doppler effect to distinguish between fixed and moving targets. There is less scope to use advanced digital signal processing techniques to reduce the effect of wind farms on marine radars and trials have indicated that wind farms produce blind areas in which other turbines and vessels could not be detected unless the observing vessel was moving (Howard and Brown, 2004). Also the high wind turbine structures produced large echoes and the radar response was strong enough to produce extraneous multiple and reflected echoes.

The effect of offshore wind farms on birds was considered in four main categories by Drewitt and Langston, 2006; collisions, displacement due to disturbance, barrier effects and habitat loss. Although the evidence was not complete, and a number of the wind farms studied were built away from large concentrations of birds, there was limited evidence of collision mortality. Similarly there was limited evidence of displacement due to disturbance but some barrier effect was reported from Horns Rev and Nysted wind farms. Loss of habitat from onshore installations (substations) and in shallow waters was highlighted as being of particular concern.

A comprehensive environmental monitoring programme was undertaken at the two Danish offshore wind farms at Horns Rev (160 MW, 14-20 km offshore) and Nysted (166 MW, 10 km offshore) between 2000 and 2006 (DONG Energy et al., 2006). Comprehensive environmental monitoring programmes investigated the impact of the wind farms construction and operation on:

  • Benthic flora and fauna, and in particular the impact of the foundations and scour protection.

  • Distribution of fish around the wind farm and impact of electro-magnetic fields on fish.

  • Behaviour of marine mammals and their reaction to the wind farm, including construction.

  • The numbers and distribution of feeding and resting birds and the impact on migrating birds including risks of collisions.

The wind farms used hard scour protection on the sandy sediment seabed and this resulted in a more diverse surface and an increase in the biomass of the benthic communities by 50-150 times. There was little evidence of any effect of the wind farm on the local fish population or of electro-magnetic fields on fish. The main impact on marine mammals (seals and porpoises) was from pile driving during the installation of the mono-pile foundations when porpoises left the area. There was evidence that birds avoid the wind farms and migration distances were extended slightly. The modelled collisions rates of eiders at Nysted were low at 0.02% (45 birds). In summary, the monitored environmental effect of these two large wind farms was limited.

An environmental monitoring programme was undertaken at two early UK offshore wind farms, North Hoyle and Scroby Sands. Each consisted of thirty 2 MW turbines directly connected to the \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) land-based power system with no offshore substation. North Hoyle wind farm is 4-5 miles off the North Wales coast and Scroby Sands 2 miles off the east coast of England. The environmental monitoring at North Hoyle, two years after commissioning, indicated small-scale changes to marine sediment composition, benthic ecology and bird distribution (DTI, 2006a). The trends could not be attributed to the wind farm and the overall conclusion was that there were no significant environmental effects due to the wind farm's construction and two years of operation.

The monitoring programme at Scroby Sands (DTI, 2006b) included bathymetric surveys and analysis around the turbines and the route of the export cables. There were also surveys of seal and little tern populations. The bathymetric surveys identified scour pits of up to \(5\mathrm{\;m}\) depth and \({60}\mathrm{\;m}\) diameter around some wind turbines and these were back-filled with rocks. There was also evidence that the submarine cable depth of laying (initially \(3\mathrm{\;m}\) ) was changing with seabed conditions and rock mattresses were placed to protect the export cables from becoming exposed or damaged. The dynamics of scour around mono-pile foundations and scour protection with data from five offshore wind farms is reviewed in DECC (2008).

docs.title: 11.8 Offshore power collection and transmission
docs.text:
The first demonstration offshore wind farms were small and used simple, well proven wind turbines typically of \({500} - {600}\mathrm{{kW}}\) rating, often stall regulated with fixed speed induction generators. The power collection voltage was \({10} - {11}\mathrm{{kV}}\) with the submarine power collection cables, a few kilometres in length, directly connected to the on-shore electrical power system. This voltage was increased to \({30} - {36}\mathrm{{kV}}\) with the use of higher rated (e.g. 2 MW) variable speed turbines offshore but the connection to shore was still at the array power collection voltage. Then larger wind farms were constructed that required the use of offshore substations to increase the voltage for transmission to shore (to \({132} - {150}\mathrm{{kV}}\) ). Offshore wind projects continue to increase in size and distance from land with one installation using a \({400}\mathrm{{MW}} \pm {150}\mathrm{{kV}}\) voltage source converter HVDC link to bring the power from several wind farms some \({200}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) to the grid connection point.

After the very early demonstration offshore wind farms, the electrical systems of offshore wind farms can be considered in three phases, corresponding to the three Rounds of UK offshore wind farm development. The division into three Rounds is due only to the administrative licensing process that was adopted by the UK but does reflect the development of offshore power collection and transmission systems (Figure 11.56).

  • In Round 1, the offshore wind farms, each with 30 turbines, were of 60-90 MW capacity and less than \({30}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) from shore. It was then possible to use the wind farm power collection voltage of \({30} - {36}\mathrm{{kV}}\) , to take the power ashore using two or three cables in parallel.

  • The Round 2 offshore wind farms were larger (up to 500 MW) but less than \({90}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) from shore. Connection to shore was possible at AC but offshore substations were needed to increase the transmission voltage up to \({132} - {150}\mathrm{{kV}}\) .

Figure 11.56 Options for offshore wind farm transmission

  • Round 3 projects are now being planned and are up to \({1000}\mathrm{{MW}}\) and \({300}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) from shore. These are likely to use AC to collect the power from the wind farms and then multiple HVDC transmission links to bring it to shore.

In all cases a transformer and its associated switchgear is located within each turbine tower to increase the generator voltage of approximately 690 V up to \({30} - {36}\mathrm{{kV}}\) . The power collection array cables enter the offshore wind turbine through a J tube, attached to the transition piece of the monopile support structures, and the temperature of the short length of cable in the J tube determines its rating. The turbine transformer, often dry cast-resin type, is located in the tower together with the turbine \({30} - {36}\mathrm{{kV}}\) switchgear. In some larger turbines the turbine transformer has been located at the top of the tower to reduce the size, weight and losses of the pendant cable. For the largest wind turbines, consideration is also being given to increasing the voltage of the array power collection system to \({72}\mathrm{{kV}}\) and the generator/variable speed equipment to either 3.3 kV or \(6\mathrm{{kV}}\) .

docs.title: 11.8.1 Offshore wind farm transmission
docs.text:
To obtain the power transfer capacity required, Round 1 UK offshore wind farms used multiple \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) cable circuits in parallel each taking up to 30-40 MW (600-800 Amps). \({}^{2}\) The wind turbines were connected in array strings and the three-phase submarine power collection cables extended to the shore where they were joined to land underground cables at a transition joint before entering a \({33}/{132}\mathrm{{kV}}\) substation.

\({}^{2}\) A small number of the more remote Round 1 offshore wind farms (e.g. Barrow) used an offshore substation but most avoided this cost by using multiple power transmission cables at the power collection voltage.

Figure 11.57 Typical UK Round 2 offshore wind farm power collection and transmission

Figure 11.57 shows a typical Round 2 offshore wind farm electrical system. Radial 33 kV \({\mathrm{{XLPE}}}^{3}\) array power collection cables with a capacity of 30-40 MW were used to connect up to eight turbines to an offshore sub-station. The conductor diameter of these cables was often tapered away from the sub-station. The sub-station was used to connect the array cables and transform the collection voltage up from \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) to \({132}\mathrm{{kV}}\) for transmission to shore. Substations of up to 90 MVA capacity typically used one offshore transformer. Larger offshore sub-stations had multiple transformers to reduce the weight of individual items of equipment and allow the wind farm to continue to operate (at less than rated output) with one transformer out of service. There was normally an auxiliary diesel generator on the offshore substation platform. The power collection circuits used three-core XLPE cable for ease of laying and to reduce environmental impact.

The transmission circuits to shore also used three-core XLPE cables, usually at \({132} - {150}\mathrm{{kV}}\) but the use of \({220}\mathrm{{kV}}\) has also been considered. Submarine AC cables \(\left( {{800}{\mathrm{\;{mm}}}^{2}\mathrm{{Cu}}}\right)\) have capacities of approximately \({200}\mathrm{{MVA}}\) at \({132}\mathrm{{kV}}\) and \({330}\mathrm{{MVA}}\) at \({220}\mathrm{{kV}}\) . Once on land, a transition joint was used to connect the three-core submarine cables to three single-core underground cables. In some cases there was also an overhead line section before the cables connected to an onshore substation. The onshore sub-station was often located tens of kilometres from shore and included reactive compensation and harmonic filters.

Specialist equipment is required for handling and laying offshore cables both within the wind turbine array and for transmission of the power to shore with \({220}\mathrm{{kV}}\) submarine high voltage cable weighing up to \({100}\mathrm{\;{kg}}/\mathrm{m}\) . Figure 11.58 shows the Lillgrund 3 core, \({400}{\mathrm{\;{mm}}}^{2}\mathrm{{Cu}},{130}\mathrm{{kV}}\) offshore transmission cable of length \(7\mathrm{\;{km}}\) from the offshore substation (Figure 11.59) to land. Note the fibre optic communications cores within the cable.

\({}^{3}\) XLPE, Cross Linked Poly Ethylene insulated cables.

Figure 11.58 130 kV submarine transmission cable used at Lillgrund offshore wind farm. Lillgrund Pilot Project, 2008. Reproduced by permission of Vattenfall; cable manufactured by ABB HVC in Karlskrona, Sweden

Figure 11.59 Offshore sub-station at Lillgrund. Lillgrund Pilot Project, 2008. Reproduced by permission of Vattenfal. See Plate 8 for the colour figure

Round 3 offshore wind farm projects have yet to be constructed but the largest projects (e.g. Dogger Bank has a total wind turbine capacity of 9000 MW with a cable route length of \({200}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) ) are likely to use HVDC transmission.

Comprehensive electrical system studies are required for the design of wind farm electrical offshore systems. For the Lillgrund project the following studies were undertaken (Lillgrund Pilot Project, 2008): cable sizing, load flow, short circuits. harmonics, grounding, voltage fluctuations, reliability, arc faults, dynamic simulation, protection coordination, insulation coordination, electromagnetic interference, lightning protection.

On land, electrical transmission systems deliver electrical energy to customers, some of whom have very high value loads and so need a reliable supply of power. Redundant circuits are installed to ensure that a single electrical fault, or sometimes two independent faults, does not result in loss of supply. In contrast the function of a wind farm offshore transmission system is to deliver wind generated electricity. The high costs of equipment offshore, particularly of submarine cables, and relatively modest value of the electrical energy mean that, as with onshore wind farms, total redundancy of circuits cannot be justified. Instead, partial redundancy can be provided for components with a high chance and/or a high impact of failure. An example is where two transformers, each of 50 or 70% of the wind farm capacity are installed. In this case, if one transformer fails only a small fraction of the energy is curtailed, as the wind farm will only operate at its full output a small fraction of the year.

A cost-benefit analysis was undertaken to determine the most cost-effective architecture for the connection of UK Round 2 offshore wind farms (Djapic and Strbac, 2008). This study balanced the costs of the offshore transmission system including those of; the submarine transmission cable(s), the offshore platform (including transformers, reactive compensation and switchgear), onshore circuits and capitalised costs of corrective maintenance against the capitalised costs of expected constrained energy due to equipment failures and maintenance as well as the cost of losses over the project life. The results showed that, similarly to land based wind farms, circuits for the transmission of offshore wind energy should be designed without explicit redundancy. Equipment failures in transmission circuits offshore require much longer repair times than those on-shore (e.g. the mean time to repair of an offshore transformer was assumed to be six months) but the cost of offshore equipment is so high that no redundancy in either transformers or submarine cables could be justified. Large offshore wind farms require multiple AC cable circuits due to the limited rating of submarine cables. Also the wind farm will be operating at its full output for only a fraction of the year. Thus, although the transmission link is designed with no redundant capacity its security is quite high. A calculation of a 600 MW offshore wind farm with \(3 \times {132}\mathrm{{kV}}\) submarine cables indicated that failure of one cable would only result in \(8\%\) of the annual wind farm energy being curtailed. It may even be cost-effective to choose a transmission link capacity that is slightly lower than the simple summation of the full power ratings of all the wind turbines if they are dispersed over a wide area.

High voltage AC cables have a limited useful route length due to their capacitance and the reactive power they generate. Hence, for the large remote wind farms of Round 3 it becomes more cost effective to use HVDC if the cable route length exceeds \({60} - {90}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) (the precise break-even point when HVDC transmission becomes more cost-effective than AC transmission depends on wind farm rating and commercial factors influencing the price of equipment).

docs.title: 11.8.2 Submarine AC cable systems
docs.text:
Large offshore wind farms have very extensive networks of submarine AC cable for power collection and transmission to shore. The \({30} - {36}\mathrm{{kV}}\) power collection circuits as well as the 132-150 kV transmission to shore cables are unusual in being very long and without any significant load connected to them. Similar cable systems are not found in land based public electricity supply systems. The electrical systems of very large, land based wind farms, such as those found in parts of China and the USA, change from underground cable within the wind farm to overhead line as soon as is practicable in order to reduce cost.

The high voltage submarine cables use solid XLPE insulation with a high dielectric value. Hence, they have much higher shunt (parallel) capacitance than overhead lines that use air for their insulation. Thus, offshore wind farm cable circuits are unique and require particular consideration.

At \({50}/{60}\mathrm{\;{Hz}}\) , the high shunt capacitance with the high system voltage results in generation of reactive power (VARs) that reduces the capacity of the circuit to transmit real power and also increases the network voltage. The no-load reactive power generation of a cable is given by:

\[ Q = {2\pi flC}{V}^{2} \]

where \(f\) is the system frequency, \(V\) is the rated voltage, and \(l\) is the length of cable. \(C\) is the capacitance of the cable per unit length.

Figure 11.60 shows the per-phase approximate equivalent circuit of a \(1\mathrm{\;{km}}\) length of \({132}\mathrm{{kV}}\) cable. It will generate approximately \(1\mathrm{{MVAr}}\) when no power is transmitted through it. This reactive power increases the voltage at the wind farm and also uses part of the thermal rating of the cable. The voltage rise is controlled by reactive power compensation equipment, usually a fixed shunt reactor on the offshore platform and a STATCOM or SVC at the on-shore substation.

In addition to reactive power generation at fundamental frequency (50 or \({60}\mathrm{\;{Hz}}\) ), the shunt capacitance of the large cable networks has important effects at harmonic frequencies.

Figure 11.61 shows the calculated impedance, seen from the \({132}\mathrm{\;{kV}}\) busbar, of the network of Figure 11.62 at harmonic frequencies. There are a number of series and parallel resonances caused by the interaction of the cable capacitance and inductive reactance of the cables and transformer. The resonances appear as low impedances (series resonance) and high impedances (parallel resonance). The harmonic resonant frequencies vary in frequency and magnitude depending on the number of cables and turbines in service (King and Ekanayake, 2010).

Figure 11.60 Per-phase approximate equivalent circuit of \(1\mathrm{\;{km}}\) of \({132}\mathrm{\;{kV}}\) cable

Figure 11.61 Impedance of the network of Figure 11.60 seen from \({132}\mathrm{\;{kV}}\) busbar

The voltage of all land based power systems contains harmonics, caused by the currents drawn by non-linear loads. Hence harmonic filters may be required at the on-shore substation to ensure that harmonic resonances within the wind farm network are not excited by this preexisting distortion. In addition variable speed wind turbines using power electronic converters and power electronic reactive compensation equipment, such as STATCOMs, inject harmonic currents into the cable networks. If these harmonics are amplified they may cause significant voltage stresses in the offshore network and may also create complex interactions with the power electronic control systems causing unpredicted equipment malfunction.

Transient over-voltages in offshore wind farm networks are generally caused by circuit breaker operation unlike in land based overhead line systems where lightning is the main cause (Lars Liljestrand, 2007). Vacuum circuit breakers are often used to control the MV networks in offshore wind farms, due to their high reliability and low maintenance requirements. In some cases vacuum circuit breakers can give multiple pre-strikes and re-ignitions and hence high-frequency transient currents. The extensive cable systems in offshore wind farms combined with a large number of step-up transformers results in many voltage reflections. The surge impedance of cables is less than \({40\Omega }\) , whereas for overhead lines it is typically \({300} - {400\Omega }\) and a lower surge impedance results in a higher rate of rise of the transient over-voltage. Thus, the extensive cable systems of offshore wind farms can lead to high transient over-voltages and demanding requirements for the circuit breakers. It may also be necessary to fit surge arrestors to protect the wind turbine transformers from switching over-voltages.

Figure 11.63 shows a simulation of the voltage of the \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) collection cable of an offshore wind farm after it is energised by a vacuum circuit breaker.

Longer lasting temporary over-voltages may occur if the main circuit breaker at the onshore connection point disconnects the wind farm from the rest of the transmission network, so that the operating wind farm and HV cable become isolated (Akhmatov, 2006; Wiechowski, 2008). Depending on the protection system of the wind turbines, they may continue to inject active current into the isolated network, charging its capacitance. Once the turbines disconnect, the energy stored in the long AC cable capacitance and the shunt reactor inductance can oscillate with a low frequency, leading to high overvoltages lasting for several seconds. If this case is considered likely, overvoltage protection which is able to absorb the energy from the cable/reactor system may be required.

Although there are relatively few large offshore wind farms in operation at present, there has been a high rate of transformer failures reported. In two offshore wind farms the turbine transformers were replaced after a large number of failures and in another offshore wind farm, a failure of the main offshore transformer led to a four and a half month outage of the entire wind farm. The reasons for these failures were complex and the transient performance of these very extensive cable systems is still the subject of research. However, it is possible that high frequency, high voltage switching transients made a significant contribution to these insulation failures. Hence, proper coordination of surge-protective devices with the insulation strength of electrical power equipment is essential for protecting the offshore electrical system from over-voltages (IEEE PES Wind Plant Collector System Design Working Group (2009)).

Figure 11.62 Typical offshore wind farm AC connection

Figure 11.63 Voltage propagating through a wind turbine power collection radial circuit during energisation. Reproduced by permission of R. King

docs.title: 11.8.3 HVDC transmission
docs.text:
For cable route lengths above \({50}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) , HVDC transmission becomes a viable option (Koch and Retzmann, 2010). Above around \({100}\mathrm{\;{km}}\) HVDC is the only option since there will be a length limit of HVAC transmission due to the high levels of reactive power generated. For wind farms above around \({200}\mathrm{{MW}}\) in size, HVDC transmission tends to have the lowest number of cables connecting the wind farm to shore.

There are two distinct HVDC technologies, Line-Commutated Current Source Converters (CSC) and Self-Commutated Voltage Source Converters (VSC), Table 11.9. CSC technology is based on line-commutated devices such as thyristors that are switched on by a pulse and switch off when the current flowing through them reduces to zero. The converters have a requirement to be connected to a strong AC system, since the AC system voltage forces the current to commutate from one phase to another. The current must always flow in the same direction through a thyristor which means that in order to change the direction of the power flow the voltage polarity of the converters must be reversed.

Table 11.9 Comparison between HVDC CSC and HVDC VSC

HVDC CSCHVDC VSCLine-Commutated Current-Sourced Converter (LCC/CSC)Self-Commutated Voltage-Sourced Converter (SCC/VSC)Turn-on capability only (Thyristors)Semiconducting switches with Turn-on and Turn-off capability (IGBTs)Low switching frequency (50/60 Hz)High switching frequency (~1000 Hz)Lower losses (~0.8% per terminal at full power)Higher losses (~1.8% per terminal at full power)Commutation within the converter is driven by the AC voltages (requires a minimum short-circuit power). A STATCOM is required offshore to provide this AC voltage reference if LCC is to be used offshore.Do not require a commutating system voltage.High space requirements, mainly due to filter requirements (to limit harmonics and to provide reactive power control)Low space requirementsConverters absorb reactive powerIndependent control of Active and Reactive powerIn service since 1954In service since 1997Installed capacity $>$ 70 GWInstalled capacity $\sim 1\mathrm{{GW}}$Highest voltage; ±800 kV DCHighest voltage; ±400 kV DCLargest scheme; 6400 MW (overhead line)Largest scheme; 400 MVA (cable)

HVDC VSC uses semiconductor switches that can be turned on and off in a controlled manner which means that HVDC VSC is able to operate when there is no local generation and it can control the AC system voltage and frequency. The majority of HVDC VSC converters in operation at present switch between two or three voltage levels to create the AC terminal voltage of the converter. However, in order to reduce switching losses, Modular Multilevel Converter (MMC) designs for HVDC VSC are now becoming commercially available.

Whilst conventional CSC HVDC is well developed with lower capital costs and losses compared to the VSC technology, there is a significantly greater foot-print of the harmonic filters. VSC technology offers greater flexibility in terms of real and reactive power control and can be used with variable speed wind turbines (see Figure 11.64). VSC has been used for the only HVDC connection to an offshore wind farm commissioned to date.

Figure 11.64 VSC HVDC transmission from an offshore wind farm

docs.title: 11.9 Operation and access
docs.text:
Access to wind farms offshore and hence maintaining high availability of the turbines is more difficult and expensive than for onshore wind farms. In many onshore wind farms, the tracks that are installed for access by large cranes during construction are maintained for the life of the project. Even if these have to be removed after construction then personnel access to the tower bases using light vehicles is straightforward and the large cranes can be re-mobilised and the access tracks reinstated if that is necessary. In contrast, the construction of offshore wind farms is undertaken using specialist vessels that, once the installation is complete, can be difficult and expensive to re-mobilise. Offshore wind turbines typically contain a light hoist for smaller items within the nacelle and may also include provision for the installation of a larger internal crane for major items of the drive trains. A gearbox or generator can then be replaced without mobilising a crane vessel. Replacing a damaged blade is likely to require a crane vessel (Amec Energy, 2004).

Access by personnel is required for routine maintenance, fault diagnosis and rectification with each wind turbine likely to require 10-20 person access visits per year. In addition to fault rectification, planned visits will be made for six and twelve month servicing of the turbines as well as various inspections for insurance and safety requirements. A minimum of a team of three is required for work to be undertaken on an offshore wind turbine. Twiddell and Gaudiosi (2009) estimate a total number of person access visits to offshore wind farms by 2010 of 200,000 per year. The early experience of the Horns Rev wind farm confirmed the need for frequent personnel access while there were 10,000 transfers between boat and tower during the construction and first two years of operation at North Hoyle wind farm (DTI, 2006a). Such frequent personnel access obviously requires safe and reliable means by which the turbines can be visited.

A number of access techniques have been tried. At Horns Rev frequent use was made of helicopters that did not land but lowered maintenance staff onto the top of the nacelle. More commonly, ladder and boat fender systems are used whereby a boat presses against tubular steel fenders attached to the wind turbine foundation and the technician transfers to and from a ladder. A number of other methods for transfer from the boat to the wind turbine have been investigated including dynamically controlled platforms. Catamarans are used in some wind farms as despite being more expensive than single hull boats they are more stable and have greater deck space.

UK experience indicates that transfers are possible with a significant wave height of up to \({1.5}\mathrm{\;m}\) using a ladder and boat fender system, depending on the wind and sea conditions. This then allows access to the turbines for 50-80% of the year (EWEA, 2009). At Scroby Sands (DTI, 2006b) the number of days when visits to the wind farm were not possible dropped from 143 (39% of the year) in the first year of operation to 76 (21%) in the second year as experience was gained and different access arrangements used. However, access during the winter months of high wind speed and hence revenue generation is limited by the wind and sea conditions and so for many wind farms there are continuing efforts to increase access up to \({90}\%\) of the year, for example through improvement of access systems using catamarans and dynamically controlled transfer platforms. Higher rates of access are likely to be prohibitively expensive and, therefore, there are also continual efforts to improve the availability of the wind turbines through the use of SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) and remote condition monitoring (see Section 11.4). A number of simulation models to assess maintenance strategies of offshore wind farms have been developed. These use probabilistic representations of the weather, and hence access to the turbines, as well as failure of components and repair times.

Table 11.10 shows the performance of two early UK offshore wind farms during the initial two years of their operation. Both wind farms received a capital grant from the UK Government and so recorded the initial operation of the wind farm as well as undertaking an environmental monitoring programme (DTI, 2006a and 2006b).

Each wind farm of 30 wind turbines was close to shore and personnel access was with a ladder and boat fender system. The capital costs were typical of the rather low costs of offshore wind farms at that time. Subsequently costs of offshore wind farms rose considerably (Gross et al., 2010).

On both sites mono-pile foundations were used. At North Hoyle a drive-drill installation technique was used with the mono-pile driven through the upper sand and clay layer and then a drill into the underlying rock. The sandy seabed conditions at Scroby Sands did not require any drilling. In both wind farms, the piles, towers and nacelles were installed mainly by jack-up vessels that used legs extending to the sea floor to provide a stable platform. The nacelle was installed with two blades attached and the third blade fitted attached to the hub once the nacelle was in position. At Scroby Sands, the assembly of the towers and turbines took approximately 12 hours with two turbines being installed every three-four days.

At both sites the availability was below the level that had been planned. There was a planned three-day grid outage at North Hoyle and at Scroby Sands one of the submarine-land cable joints failed resulting in one of the \({33}\mathrm{{kV}}\) circuits being out of commission for 12 weeks. A number of bearings were replaced in situ on both the generators and gearboxes at North Hoyle while at Scroby Sands all the generators were replaced and replacement of some gearbox bearings was required. At Scroby Sands additional remote monitoring was installed in order to increase availability.

The operation and maintenance costs to the project operators were £10-13 per MWh although as this was during the warranty period a number of costs relating to availability and unscheduled maintenance were borne by the manufacturer (estimated at one third of the operating costs). This agrees with the estimate of the Opti-EWECs project (van Bussel et al., 2010) that operation and maintenance costs of offshore wind farms might be some 25% of the levelised costs of energy.
